From his study of these Dr. Sorby reached the remarkable conclusion that these granite rocks, now at the surface, must have been at the time of their formation covered by several miles of super-incumbent rock. That this has been removed so as to expose the granites indicates the stupendous amount of denudation which has taken place.
PEAT COKE MADE IN BAVARIA.

Peat coke manufacture by the Ziegler pro- cess has been started at Beuerberg, Bavaria. The peat is cut up, pressed, and exposed to the air until evaporation has reduced its water to less than 23 per cent, of the whole mass. This peat is then placed in a retort for eighteen hours. The coke is finally re- ceived in air-tight iron cars, which are left for six or eight hours to cool before they are discharged. Each retort yields during every twenty-four hours eight to ten tons of coke. The gas is pa.Asedi through various, tanks and towers in which the by-products are sepa- rated, and is then employed in assisting the retort process which could not even com- mence without the external application of heat.

div.head: SIZE OF THE MABIBIOTH.
div.p: THE SIZE OF THE MABIBIOTH.

Exaggerated ideas have been entertained, according to the opinion of Mr. F. A. Lucas, concerning the prodigious size of the ancient mammoths, whose remains have been found in Alaska and Siberia. It is a Mistake, he says, to ascribe to them a greater size than that of the modern elephant. He believes that no Siberian mammoth has been found with a greater height, at the shoulders, than 9ft. 6in. Indian elephants occasionally attain this height, whereas the African elephant often stands lift, at the shoulders, and some- times slightly more. The real giants among fossil elephants were found in Southern Europe and the Western and South-Western parts of the United States. These stood "from 12ft. 6in., to possibly 13ft. 6in r high."

div.head: CRYSTALLISATION AND HARDNESS.
div.p: CRYSTALLISATION AND HARDNESS.
When •we speak of a metal being in a crystalline state, we almcst invariably asso- ciate that state with the idea of hardness. Even practical metallurgists entertain this

notion, although, as Mr. G. T. Beilby saysol in a paper read before the Royal Society in London. "in the pure ductile metals the crystalline state is actually ,the soft state." A large part of this softness is ascribed to the instability of the crystalline structure. When a metal is drawn into wire its tenacity is enormously increased; that of iron four times,,* that of pure gold more than three times, and that of silver and copper still more. But investigation shews that metals which have been thus treated slam a micro- structure in which deformed and broken- (town crystals are embedded in a non- crystalline mass. In the process of harden- ing a metal, its crystalline structure is broken down, and it passes into the non- crystalline form,

div.head: DIAMONDS AND METEORS.
div.p: DIAMONDS AND METEORS.

The diainond has always possessed such a fascination for the human mind that it is no wonder a Celestial origin has often been at- tributed to it, and at least ,pne eminent physicist—Meydenhauer--was of 'opinion that the sparkling gems descended from the sky in the form of a meteoric shower. This, ac- * cording to an Article in the North American Review, is not so improbable as it may seem, - and would appear to receive confirmation in • the State of Arizona, where, extending over an area of about five miles, there are some

thousands of blocks of iron varying in weight from a gramme to half a ton, and un- .doubtedly of meteoric origin. It is not known at what period this dangerous meteoric shower fell upon the earth. A mineralogist who broke one of these blocks of iron found
inside a eutatance much harder than metallic

iron, and on subjecting it to a chemical ahalysis he discovered that it was a black diamond. Its presence demonstrated that the meteorites had at some time or other tra- versed a temperature eqti ii to that of an elec- tric furnace.

div.head: SURE 'TEST OF DEATH.
div.p: A SURE 'TEST OF DEATH.

Dr.'Ascarelli Attilio draws attention to the difficulty of ascertaining whether death .has really taken place, which has been re. .cognised in Germany by attaching to every cemetery a mortuary room in which every body is retained for a certain number of hours before burial, while attached to it are instruments of precision which will give warning of the slightest movement. The doc- tor has made an extended series of experi- ments on dogs to ascertain whether the acidification of the tissues of the body, which takes place soon after death, cannot be made use of as an exact demonstration of -death. He gives it as .his conclusion that this acidification does take place uniformly in the tissues, so that its occurrence may be regarded as an infallible sign of real death. It is the first symjitom of death appearing in thirty-five minutes after the cessation of the heart beats. Acidity appears first in the. spleen, kidneys, heart, and liver. The cause of death makes certain variations in the phenomena, but the rapidity of death has no effect on acidification.

div.head: MICROSCOPIC STRUCTURE OF METALS.
div.p: MICROSCOPIC STRUCTURE OF METALS.

To Dr. Sorby is also due the initiation of the application of the microscope to the ex- amination of the structure of steels. This method, which consists in studying the minute structure revealed by the microscope in a piece of highly-polished metal, has been of very great practical importance. It has re- volutionised the science of metallurgy. of arn)Crt it may be said to nave created a new branch which may be called metallography. It has been applied with much success to the study of alloys.

div.head: " MILK " FROM FISH.
div.p: " MILK " FROM FISH.

Many cuttle fish farms—great tanks where the fish are bred for their black milk, which gives us India ink—are to be found on the Chinese coast, observes the Reader. To milk a cuttle fish, the queer creature is driven slowly and gently into a compartment or lock lined with metal. Then the water is gradu- ally drawn off, and the fish in the end finds himself left high and dry. He becomes alarmed, and squirts forth all the sepia in his sack. Then, milked dry, he is returned to his tank again.

div.head: FORESTS AND WIND VELOCITY.
div.p: FORESTS AND WIND VELOCITY.

M. St. Murat, director of the Meteorologi- cal Institute of Roumania, has published the results of his study of the retarding influence of forests on wind velocity in the Annales of the Roumanian Academy. He Ends that the greatest effect which a forest can have upon the wind consists in diminishing the wind velocity to leeward of the forest. At 164 ft. this decrease in velocity may amount to 4 to 7-1 miles an hour, which means a reduction of the force of the wind by ldeg. on the Beau- fort scale. This decrease is felt within 330 ft. of the forest. After that the velocity in- creases again with increasing distance, and at about 1,640 ft. reaches the force noted before the forest was encountered.

div.head: STRONGEST OF ALL WOODS.
div.p: STRONGEST OF ALL WOODS.

Official tests of the many valuable hard woods native to Western Australia have made known the extraordinary properties of yate, believed to be the strongest of all known woods. Its average tensile strength is 24,0001 b. to the square inch, equalling that of good cast iron. Many specimens are, how- ever, much stronger, and one was tested up to seventeen, and a-half tons to the square inch, which is equal to the tensile strength of wrought iron. The sawn timber of yate is ,probably the strongest in the world. The tree grows to a maximum height of 100 ft., and has sometimes a diameter of 2ift. or even 3ft.

It will be glorious to get away, out of this wretched lodging "—glancing summer shades. The coat, which comes a little round the shabby parlour—"and go into a nice, below the hips, is of the close semi-fitting variety, well-appointed house, with money to buy pretty things, and nothing to do." • "Bless the child! "—patting her hand affec- titonately. ".You do hate work. You're not like
By CLARA MULHOLLAND,

I was close. In the mean little street into which she gazed, poor, weary-looking men and women I tramped slowly to and fro. Dirty children ; played together in the gutter; lazy boys hung ; round the doorsteps and area railings. Seen ; though panes of glass thick with dust and grime, the prospect was not a lively one, and Honor's heart felt low.

"The Fulham-road will be little better," she thought, sighing. "To get away to sunny lands; to see new places,;how glorious it would be! And yet-- No; I won't give' up my appoint- ment. Uncle Roger is good, kind, generous. But two people are enough. And the money--" She turned suddenly, and of the struggle that had been going On in her mind there was not the smallest sign in her earnest little face, as she , bent and kissed her mother's cheek.

"I'm delighted that uncle Roger has sent for you dear," she aid, gently. "And I hope you and Pauline will have a good time." "Honor! And why should we only have a good time ? Surely you--" "Surely I will havo a good time, too—but at home, mother. Two are better than three, in every way "—she breathed unusually hard. "The money will go farther. And I can't, at present anyway, give up my appointment. So--" "It doe l seem a pity. But still, I'd like you to get married, Honor. And what chance has a dispenser ? " Honor laughed, and patted her mother's cheek. "I'm no beauty. And—well, there's an old saying: `Shut a girl up in a bandbox, ahe'll meet with her fate. So who knows what may happen, even at the hospital. So "—gaily—"don't fret. My fate, at present, is splendid. I'll be independent and self-supporting." "It's not fair. Uncle Roger won't be pleased." "Yes he will. And I tell you what, mother. I "—With a sudden, sweet smile—"will go out for Paulina's wedding, and stay on with you then. Now "—turning to her sister—"isn't that a good arrangement?" "Yes." Paulina thought Honor foolish and quixotic, but the recollection that if the girl stayed at home, she would have a full hundred to spend on the adornment of her own pretty person, made her keep her ideas to herself. 'And if you really don't mind, dear, it--" "Mind! We need not discuss that," cried Honor, and after a few useless and faltering objections from her mother, the whole thing was settled. Mrs. Carrington and Pauline were to sail for India 'as soon as possible. Honor was to take up her appointment at the Ophthalmic Hospital, in the Fulham-road.

"A wild ,wind and a bright sun.. Clouds of dust flying round the street corners. Thank you, Max, the house is the place for me to-day. -You must go out alone." "'A bushel of March dust is worth a King's ransom,' Elinor, and the Bun is warm and--" " 'A speck of March dust maketh the eye '-- No that is not a proverb," laughed Elinor. "But I'm immovable. In the house I stay." "You'll be bored to extinction, alone."

"That "—with a plaintive little sigh, and the sudden raising of her delicately-pencilled brow. —"is my normal condition." "You want something to do, Elinor. An interest of some kind." "Where am I to get it? I've everything I want in one way now. And yet "—a deep blush overspread her fair face—"it seems to me— But run off, Max. You love the sun, and have no veil and things to suffer from the wind. So go. `Stand not upon the order of your going,' as the immortal Shakespeare says, `but go." "It's time, when you throw sayings from Macbeth at my head. I'm gone." Andi laughing, Maxwell Leonard left the handsome house in Sloane-gardens, which he and his sister had lately furnished, and walked quickly down the street.

, "Poor Elinor," he sighed presently. "Will her affairs ever come right, I wonder? Will that fellow ever turn up again? Till he does I fear she'll never be happy. We're rich, tlncl does, -all we want now. But so long as Fairfax is missing Elinor will be miserable. What a strange thing , love is, to be sure. People talk of it as bliss. Well "—laughing—"it has often the appearance of something very different. However I can't speak, since I've never experienced the feeling. ,I m a hardened old sinner, I sdppose, for airs and graces, and sweet, pretty faces don't move me one bit. By Jove! What a blast!" And he clutched wildly at his hat as, on turning into the Fulham-road, a sudden gust of wind nearly carried it off. "And such dust! If a bushel's worth a King's ransom,' what's all this worth ? Ah!" He gave a little cry of pain, and stood still, fumbling blindly for his pocket-handker- chief.

; A speck of dust in your eye? Painful thing," I said a young man, sympathetically, at his elbow. "Let me take you to the Ophthalmic Hospital; ,there a doctor'll whip it out in a jiffy." "You're a real good Samaritan. Take me where you will," laughed Max, his face screwed up. "This March dust is a scourge, if you like." 1 "Yet it's worth a King's ransom, they say." "A bushel—not a speck. Ah! is this the place? Not up to much, as far as looks go. In spite of this treasure in my eye, I can see that." _ _ _

, "I wouldn't judge by appearances," laughed the stranger. "You'll be blessing it, shabby as it is, before long. Doctor in?" he asked the porter who opened the door in aver to his ring at.: the bell. "This gentleman has got a hasty piece of dust in his eye." "Very sorry, sir," the Man replied, "every doctor's gone. But I have it. The dispenser'll do all you want. Come in, gentlemen." "Thank you, I'll leave him to you now," the stranger said, and, bowing,.he went away. Maxwell" followed the porter into a small room, the back parlour of the house. It wee dingy and black-looking, and fitted up with several rows of dark wooden benches.

"Not much luxury here," thought Maxwell, and he dropped on to a seat, pressing his hand- kerchief across his burning oyes. "I hope this fellow will soon come, and that his hands may be clean. Dispensers are--" A light step, a firm, cool hand upon his brow, a sweet, soft voice asking him to turn a little towards the window, gave Maxwell a sudden thrill of pleasure and surprise; and as his hand- kerchief was removed, and the lid of his inflamed eye gently raised, he saw a young girl, in a fresh, blue blouse, a big holland apron enveloping her slender form, her brown hair curling low on her broad, white forehead, bending over him. In a few seconds the obnoxious particle of dust was extracted, his eyes bathed, and Maxwell stood up, grateful and delighted. He thanked the girl profusely; then looked at her with a start of recognition, and held out his hand. "Miss Carrington !" he exclaimed, quickly. Surely you have not forgotten me? I met you quite three years ago. But still—" Honor's face lit up with pleasure. "I have not forgotten you, Mr. Leonard. And I am glad to have been of use to you." "You have given me marvellous relief. But why—how are you here, Miss Carrington ? " A shadow rested for an instant on the girl's bright face. Then she looked up, and "Because I passed the examinations success- fully. You see "—quickly—"father died, and— and left us very poor. Mother and Paulina went to Uncle Roger, in India, and are having fine times."

"And you? Why didn't You go?" "Well, you see, three were rather too many. And I had my appointment. But "—gaily-41 am to go out to Paulina's wedding." "And when will,that be ? " Honor rubbed her eyes suddenly,- and a faint tinge of pink stole into her pale cheeks. There was something just a little embarrassing in Maxwell Leonard's earnest glance. "I can't say. Not for some time, however. Paulina's immensely admired, for she's very pretty. But she's not engaged yet." Ho smiled, looking as though the news both pleased and relieved his mind. "So we shan't lose you, just as we've found you? I'm glad of that," he said; then laughed as he saw an expression of surprise in the girl's frank eyes. "I say we, meaning my sister and myself. You remember Elinor, Miss Carrington ? " "Well. Is she as pretty as ever ? " "I think so. But she is pale and weary-look- . ing. We, unlike you " he reddened —"have grown rich, and the change does not quite agree with Elinor. She looks interest, and things that money can buy are not enough for her. Will you come and see her? The sight of your busy, useful life may do her good. We live quite near, in .Sloane-gardens."
"How very pleasant," Honor cried. "I'll go to see Minor with pleasure. I have plenty of spare time. This "--throwing open the door of a small room that smelt like a chemist's shop—

"is my dispensing den. I make up the doctors' prescriptions here, and hand bottles to out- patients through that little hole "—pointing to an opening in the wall. "That generally takes the afternoon. But in the morning, and the evening after seven, I am free—except on Fridays, when I am kept going till nine or ten M night. When would Elinor like to see me ? " "Any time. But "—eagerly—"come to dinner to-morrow. Elinor shall write to you, or call and see you." "You are very kind. It will be a pleasure to meet her again.
With a buoyant step and a light heart Max made his way home, and hurried to the drawing- room to look for Elinor.

"She must go at once. This girl is just the companion she wants," he told himself. "I am glad I had the good luck to meet her. So even a speck of March dust in the eye "—laughing— "is worth something." _ _ . . .

The sound of ,r'oices in the drawing-room chased the smile from his lips. "Visitors. What a nuisance! Well, perhaps they won't stay long." And, opening the door, he went in. At the window stood Elinor, a tall, dark man
by her side, and, with a start of astonishment, Maxwell recognised the good Samaritan of the Fulham-road.

"How on earth did he get here?" he asked himself, wondering. "Max!" Elinor turned —a radiant, happy Elinor now—and with outstretched hands ran forward to meet him. "Oh! I'm so glad you have come in. Here is Gerald Fairfax. He has been abroad—but has got on. And "—a wave ot crimson sweeping over her face, her voice falling to a shy whisper—"he loves me, and—and we are engaged. You do not know him, except by name, but you'll soon like him, I feel sure. Congratu- late me, dear."

"My dear Elinor! "—Max threw his arms round her— 'I wish you all joy and happiness. But"— looking towards her lover—"l do know Fairfax. I "--holding out his hand—"made his acquaint- ance to-day." Gerald shook his hand warmly. "In a funny way," he cried. "I hadn't the faintest idea '*ho - you were. I trust the dispenser was equal to the occasion." _

"Rather! Whipped the dust gat, as you said, 'in a jiffy.' " Fairfax laughed. "I'm glad he was so expert." "He? My dear fellow, it was no he, but a lady. One of the-- Elinor, you must go off at once and call:upon her." "Max!" Elinor took a step backwards and gazed at her brother with an alarmed expression. "No," Max laughed, "I'm not insane, Elly. It's dear little Honor Carrington." "Honor Carrington a dispenser of medicine ? " "Yes. Iso't it wonderful? She seemed only a child three years ago. How she learnt Latin, &c., and passed such stiff exams, beats me." "Oh, she was always clever," remarked Elinor. "But where are her people?" "In India. Go and see her, Elly, and give her some amusement."

Elinor looked closely at her brother, and then her lips parted in a sweet, well-pleased smile. "We'll make her come here to-night," she cried, joyously, "and have a nice champagne dinner for four, to celebrate Gerald's return and .our engagement. Does that please you, brother mine

"Perfectly. You're an angel, Elinor." "Not at all, only"—with a radiant glance—"a happy woman. I'd like to give dear little Honor a chance, too." Max bent down suddenly and kissed her. "Write her a note then, and I'll go back with it to the hospital." "No, no," gaily. "Not so soon, Max. Gerald and I are going for a walk. We'll see Honor, and make her promise to come." "But the wind is high, Elinor," cried Max, "and the dust--" "Never mind," laughing. "If I do get a speck in my eye, Gerald will lead me to the hospital, and the talented dispenser will quickly remove it. Sit down' you two, and have a friendly chat. I'm off to put on my things. Au revair." And she tripped away.

The days and weeks slipped past with wonder- ful rapidity, and .one evening, when the Indian mail came in, Honor remembered, with something like a shock, that her mother's letter had s ceased to be the important thing in her life that - it used to be. "At the beginning it was all I had to comfort- , me," she said, fastening a spray of tea-roses on the bodice of her white dinner-aress. "It is not that I care less, but "—a delicate pink creeping into her cheeks—"my days and evenings have been so full, so happy. But, alas ! that will soon be over. This will, perhaps, be our last dinner-party at Sloane-gardens. For Elinor's wedding next week must end everything. The house will be shut up. And he will, of course, go away too. Ah ! then," sighing, "this place will be changed. I wish Paulina would hurry. If she were but engaged, I'd have to go, and I'd be almost glad. But, I declare! I'll be late. I'll read mother's letter another time." And thrusting it into her pocket, she threw on a long ' cloak, gathered up her muslin skirts, and ran down to the cab that was waiting for her at the hospital door. It was a sultry evening, and when dinner was over Honor left Elinor surrounded by her lady guests, and stepped out on to the balcony. "I could see by the street lamp," she thought, "to read mother's letter. This would be a good opportunity." But before she broke the seal someone came out through the big window, and stood beside her.

With a bright blush and a sudden, quick throb of pleasure, the girl saw that it was Max. "A letter ?" he said, quickly. "I "—turning away—" am interrupting—preventing you from reading it ? " "No, no—that is—it's O.nly "—with a nervous - and rather guilty little langh—"from mother, and any time will do to read it, that is "—apolo- getically—"you see, I'm always half-afraid to find that Paulina's approaching marriage will oblige me—to go—out—there." Maxwell turned pale. "You would not wish to go surely, _Honor ? " "Oh, no!" looking up with a start. "It would ' break my heart." "And mine to see you go—that is "—he bent towards her, his eyes full of a great and passionate longing—" unless I might go also— take you there as my wife ? " "Max! "
"Honor, my darling, I love you. Can you love me always? Take me as your husband, for better for worse ?"

"Till death do us part," Honor whispered, softly. "Yes, Max—yes. And oh! I hope and pray that I may make you happy." "Of that I have not the smallest doubt, my darling," he murmured with deep emotion, and catching her hands he drew her into his arms. "And now," Honor cried after a while, and. moving away from him, "I must take a peep• at mother's letter."
"Do. Though what she says does not matter much. You ail mine now. Nothing can separate us."

Presently Honor gave a little cry of pleasure. "Max, they are coming home! Paulina is not engaged, but Uncle Roger has got his long leave. How splendid! And so "—with a soft little chuckle —"the small dispenser in the Fulham- road "-7-looking up at him with loving admiration —"has done better than the gay girl in Burmah, Max."

He slipped his arm round her waist. "There are worse places than the Fulham-road, sweet- heart." Honor's fresh laugh rang out merrily on the evening breeze. "Especially with a high wind and the dust flying into one's eyes?" "Exactly. That speck of dust, little one, Was worth more than the ransom of fifty kings to me, for it brought supreme joy and happiness into my life." [ME END.]

ST. ANN'S.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with this church was held on Tuesday evening the vicar (the Rev. Jay. Davies) in the chair. There were also present :—Messrs. E. Winter and T. H. Corbett (wardens), H. H. Bretherton, William Thomas (lay reader), J. E. Goodwin, Charles Bunch, G. ' Armstrong, Charles Bradshaw, and S. C. Daniels.—The Vicar made a sympathetic allusion to the death of Mr. E. W. Woods who had been vestry °irk since St. Ann's Church was built in 1869. 0r39 years ago.— The Vicar alluded in grateful terms to the valuable work which had been rendered during the past year by the church officers. He (the Vicar) was in a measure understaffed, as for 12 months he had been without a colleague in the ministry, although in their lay reader, Mr. Thomas, he had one who did a noble work. (Hear, hear. Allusion was made to the death of one of the sidesmen (Mr. T. Houghton) who had been associated with the church as a choir boy and then as an adult member and sidesman. They had also lost a regular subscriber in the person of Mrs. Ashton.—The Vicar re-appointed Mr. E. Winter as his warden for the ensuing year, and the vestry selected Mr. 'I. H. Bretherton were re-appointed the lay representatives to attend the .ruri-dacanal and diocesan conferences.— Mr. Armstrong was appointed vestry clerk.— A meeting of communicants was then held, the Vicar again presiding, and at which the churchwardens' accounts were presented, showing that there was a balance in hand of £lO 3s. 9id. The Vicar, in the course of another speech on the work of the church during the past year, pointed out that nearly £6OO had been spent on their day schools. Their ideas with reference to the Church Renovation Fund were somewhat expensive, but it had been found that it would be neecessary to spend from £2OO to £3OO on the ofgan to put it in a satisfactory condition. It was hoped assistance would be rendered them by Mr. Carnegie.

Warburton, Acton, Blythe, J. Grounds. Bray- shaw, and A. Grounds fot the Church, and Messrs. J. Cartwright and Firmstone for the mission. •M r. Foster presented the accounts. The offertories both general and special amounted to £179 IGs. Bd. The expenses balanced that amount within a penny. They were all very gratified in finding that they had had such a good year. The Rev. H. H. Corsbie presented the mission accounts which showed that the Ordinary collections amounted to £l7 198. 2d. and the special to .610 is. 9cl. The subscriptions amounted to £1 ss. Gd. and the expenses were £l9 15s. 6d. The Vicar said both the accounts were very satisfac- tory. The year had been a -Very long one, there being 55 Sundays in last year so that they had more collections. He thanked them for the Easter offering which was the largest for the last ten years. It was very encouraging to think one's services were appreciated and he took it that the collection was their appreciation of his services. The work of the mission church was going on extremely well— in fact it could hardly go on better. They intended having another bazaar, because they wanted a new mission church. _
The accounts were passed. A vote of thanks was accorded to the organist, the choir and the other officials of the church on-the motion of Mr. Farghar, seconded by Mr. Warburton. ST. BARNABAS' CHURCH.

The vestry meeting in connection with this church was held on Thursday evening,the Vicar (Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth) presiding over a good attendance.—The Vicar nominated Mr. Evan Evans to serve as his warden. Mr. W. A P.. kati retired from the office of people's warden and Mr. C. Skinner was elected to succeed him, on the proposition of Mr. Westwell seconded by Mr. E. Evans.—The Vicar nominated Messrs. A. J. Allen, J. Hamer and T. A. Jones as his sidesmen and Mr. Skinner nominated Messrs. J. E. Morgan, E. Liddell and B. Lester. The following were elected by the vestry Messrs. W. Boyle, G. Rolfe, J. Tomkins and J. Waring. Messrs. E. Evans and C. Skinner were appointed lay‘ representatives.—The statement of accounts,presented by Mr.Proud,showed that the income for the year amounted to £156 3s. 7d. and after making grants of £5 to the decoration fund, 5 to the Pan Anglican Congress fund, and £2O to the curate's fund, there was a balance in hand of 10s. 3d.—Votes of thanks were accorded to the officers for their past services and to the Vicar for presiding.—The Vicar commented upon the satisfactory work of the year and expressed his special pleasure at the nurnber of Easter communicants (198) which was larger than ever before. ST. THOMAS'S, STOCKTON HEATH. This vestry meeting was held at noon on Tuesday, the Vicar (Rev. J. Collins) presiding. There were also present --Messrs. Henry Greenall, T. J. Lee, F. Pear- son, T. R. Westbrook, A. J. Willett, T. Sharrocks, J. Parkes, M. H. Brady, J. A. McGregor, and C. Spencer, —Mr. Lee (people's warden) presented the statement of accounts, which showed that the total receipts amounted to £392 17s. 3d., as compared with £332 17s. sd. last year. The general offertory, including the harvest festival, totalled £243 4s. 9d. as against £228 17s. last year. There was a balance due to the wardens of £2 Is. 4d. . .

The balance sheet was adopted on the proposition of Mr. Sharrocks, seconded by Mr. Westbrook,—The following officers were re-appointed : Vicar's warden, Mr. Greenall ; people's warden, Mr. Lee; sidesmen, Messrs. W. Richardson, A. Down, J. 11.Clarke,J.Jeffes, T. R. Westbrook, J. A. McGregor, W. Mclntyre, T. Sharrocks, L. G. Davies, J. Parkes, A. J. Willett and J. Melbourne ; lay representatives, Messrs. McGregor and Sharrocks. The Vicar thanked all the officials and choir for their services.—Mr. Lee handed a cheque for £3o,the amount of the Easter o 2 fferings to the Vicar, who expressed his appreciation of the kind feeling which prompted it. Referring to the Curate Fund, he said great improve- ment had been made during the year, thanks to their. treasurers, and there was paid in the other day a sum of £l7 16s. More had bpen promised. They hoped to raise in the parish by subscriptions at least £lOO to save drawing on the capital and the holding of sales of work. _

Mr. Greenall referred to the good work done by the district visitors in collecting the money, and he moved a vote of thanks to them. This was seconded by Mr. Lee, and cordially passed.—On the proposition of the Vicar, seconded by Mr. Greenall, it was decided to send the following resolution to Mr. Balfour :—" The Education Bill as proposed by Mr. McKenna is regarded as a violation of the two great principles of liberty of the subject and liberty of the conscience, and as such calls for the most strenuous opposition of all loyal Churchmen. No measure can be regarded as satisfactory which deprives the Church of England parents of their undoubted right to have their children educated in the elementary schooleof the country in conformity with their religious convictions, by teachers approved by the Church."
There was SONO discussion at the outset as to whom to send the resolution, and Mr. Pearson caused some laughter ty observing : "Send it to Joynson Hicks. He can take it for you next week."

div.p: WALTON CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held on Easter Mon- day, the Vicar (the Rev. L. J. T. Darwall) being in the chair. The outgoing wardens, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., and Mr. William Weir were re-elected to office ; and the accounts, showing a balance in hand, were sub- mitted and passed. A warm recognitioA was made by Mr. Cooper and Mr. Yarwood and others of the efficiency of the organist and choir, and the meeting ended with a vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: GRAPPENHALL.
div.p: GRAPPENHALL.

The Easter vestry meeting was held on Tuesday morn- ing, the Rector (the Rev. H. V. Pigot) presiding. The accounts were presented by the retiring wardens, Messrs. Lister-Kaye and Leigh Leyland, and showed a credit balance of £7 7s. 3d., as against a credit balance last Easter of £2 2s. Id. The Rector nominated Mr. H. Beresford Melville as his warden, and the parishioners elected as their warden Mr. Harry Standish Leyland. It was resolved "That the gratitude of the vestry for Mr. Leigh Layland's 17 years' service as churchwarden be recorded on the minutes." Mr. G. G. Ainsworth was elected Rector's sidesmen and the parishioners elected seven sidemen, viz. :—Messrs. V. Hoskin, H. Owen, H. H. Barber, H. N. Morrey, J. Ashcroft, F. Fuller and T. Brierley. The vestry appointed Messrs. Lister-Kaye and H. B. Melville as lay representatives.

div.head: CROWN AND THE MAPLE LEAF.
div.p: THE CROWN AND THE MAPLE LEAF.

Travellers to Canada by steamers of the Allan Royal Mail Line often have occasion to note the innovations made for their increased comfort. For over half a century the Allans—a name known as widely on the other side of the Atlantic as it is on this—have initiated improvement after improvement in steamship travel, and have given attention not only to the larger matters such, for instance, as their pioneer turbine steamers, but also to those smaller details which mean so much to passengers' happiness. During the past few weeks another distinctive feature has been added to the steamers of the Line,this being the introduction into the saloons of a super-Wilton carpet of an entirely new and registered , pattern. The design consists of the Imperial Crown and the Canadian Maple leaf, these being charruinely interwoven in several shades of crimson, and giving a very rich and artistic effect. The combination of the Crown, emblamatio of the Dominion as part of the British Empire, with the Maple leaf, is particularly appropriate, and will be admired alike by , Canadian and English travellers. The carpets, it may be added,have been specially manufactured for the Align Line by Messrs. A. Blain and Son, Paradise-street Liverpool.

div.head: (Copyright) THE LIGHT ON THE CLIFF.
div.p: (Copyright) THE LIGHT ON THE CLIFF.
BY H. D. LOWRY,
Author of "Wreckers and Methodists," "IN omen's Tragedies," "A Man of Moods," &c., &c.

I was born and bred down yonder at the Cove, and there's' that in this lonely country round about Lanjestyn which has kept me from wandering all my life, . save for one period of five years, when I travelled the wide world over upon one ship or another. I had loved Sarah from a boy, and I never abandoned the hope of winning a return. But when she promised to marry George Laity, and all my hopes were ended, the place grew hateful to me. I didn't dare to say much to the old people; but I went away from the Cove a few days before her wedding, and walked to Falmouth, where I shipped for a sailor. For five long years, as I have said, I went from port to port, and all that time I had no word from home. I conld hardly expect to, t for, although I wrote and sent money sometimes, there was` a strange restlessness upon me, and I was never long aboard one ship. I tried to forget Sarah, and in the course of time I came near doing it. At least, I began to understand that her love was .one of the things I had missed in life, and must make shift to do without.

But when I had gone thus far, there was another thing began to trouole me. I began to hate the heathen folk of the foreign ports, and the drouthy heat of places that we visited. Night and day I was dreaming of the moor that lies about Lanjestyn, and the track leading down to the Cove through the heather. The, wash of the sea was different upon foreign shores from the sound that had been in my ears when I was born down there, and there was never any freshness in the air. Sarah would be an old married woman by this time, and so changed that she would make no difference to me if I went back. So at last I resolved I would go.

Now, as for George Laity, I had learnt in those years of my wandering to hope for the best about him. Even while I did not recognise a rival in him, he had been a man that I could never abide; and it was but natural that this dislike should be greater when he caused the death of my dear hopes.' But I had come to see that if Sarah had been for me he could not have parted us. Things being as they were, another would have taken her if he had not. So I supposed that he would have turned out as good a husband as need be. It was not until afterwards I heard the story of how much Sarah suffered at his hands.

It would appear that for some time after the wedding all went well. Sarah was a fine-made, spirited girl that any man might be proud to have won, and George was well pleased with himself, and all that could be expected to her.

• Like nine men out of ten that lived hereabouts in those days, he was mixed up in the smuggling; but not one in twenty had had his success. If the Revenue men came along and asked his occupation, he would point to a few acres of wastrel and call himself a farmer; but the land was mostly left to farm itself, and all the crops of a century would not have bought the silks, and laces, and brandy that were stored in "cavies " cunningly excavated in the corner of a field, or under the old trees of the orchard, or (as happened once) in the very centre of the road that led up to the farmhouse from the Cove.

Sarah could wear such clothes to church as would make the Squire's lady forget her dignity, and look across to George's pew when she should have been listening to the sermon. The little Hope was the fastest boat that ever sailed out of the Cove—she made no less than five-and-forty runs to Rusco and back in the year after the wedding—and George, who owned her, was by way of becoming the richest man :for miles around, having wonderful luck in escaping the preventive officers.

In due season a child was born, and' Sarah was like one that can't fancy there's anything in God's universe beyond what's under her own roof. Yet this child was the beginning of the unhappiness that came upon her soon after its birth.

For the little maid wa n't like the child ,of George and Sarah. They .were big-made. and handsome, the both of them, and neither of them knew what it was to 13;rill. ,The little maid was a whisht sight; sure enough, and always ailing. There were some who called to mind old tales about the piskies that 'll steal children and leave their own in place of them, for it was almost easier to believe such nonsense than to suppose that this was the child of two such parents.

However, 'tis the nature of babies to be small and weak. Sarah loved her little daughter all the better for its helplessness, and if it was always crying, it was for ever calling on her to love and comfort it, and her heart heard and understood. As for George, he did not notice its weakness for a time.

But when the child was a.little over a year old a double change began to be' visible in him. Ile vete a strong man, and violent in his temper, so that little was known at Erst of the reasons which made him turn away from Sarah, his companions fearing to speak what they knew. But she learnt very quickly that lid had ceased to love her, and afterwards that he almost hated her because he was bound to her for ever.

As to the child, the time came when he conic: scarce abide the sight of it. The little maid was still the weakling she had been at birth ; neither mind nor body grew in the natural way of children. She did not cry now. She , lay with great eyes staring out of a pale, thin face, as though she could foresee some terrible unhappiness that was to come. George Laity couldn' bear to look upon her. . .

"Was ever a man father to such a thing in all the world P" he would cry. "If she would screech I wouldn' care, but she don't do nothin' but gaze and gaze like one that can see all the past and more than all the future."

Sarah very quickly learnt to say nothing. If he hated his own child—and she saw that the uncannines's of it had brought him to that pitch of wickedness—she must find all the, more of love for it.. George didn't make fifty voyages in the veer now. He was much away, and people began to whisper of what kept him so much Icinger in Rusco than was necessary for the loading, of

cargoes. Sarah did not concern herself with the gossip of the village, but there are always kind friends to tell unpleasant tidings to those that do not wish to hear them; and, even if these had been wanting, she did not need much cleverness to interpret George's daily actions, and some part of his speech to her. So she lived miserably at the farmhouse, the little child her.only comfort and companion. -

You know the nature of the place: for miles and miles, betwixt both seas, the graves of those that died in bygone ages are commoner than the hooks of the living. There was at this time no doctor nearer than Trenear, eight miles away across the moor.

One night George Laity came home to find the place in a commotion. "George," cried Sarah, "I'm fine an' glad that you've come back. I believe the little maid is dying. She can hardly draw breath, and Miss Curgenven do tell 'me she can't do no more for her." •
George WS in a poor temper that night. He looked across the room to where an old woman, skilled in the use of herbs and such things, IVAC bending over a dark oaken cradle.

[THE END.] of the country to which I returned. Thcre was one place where badgers had dwelt from time immemorial, and I must needs descend the face of the cliff to settle a question which bad arisen in me, as to whether they had forsaken their ancient haunting-ground during the eternity of my five years' absence. It was not until dark that I made up my mind to go forward without any further wanderings from the track. 'This beaten way lies close to the edge of the cliff. Above it the land often rises slowly for the distance of a hundred yards or so. .Now, once, as I followed the track, I was aware of voices not far , away. I halted and listened. It was not possible to discover any trace of those whom I heard, but I had not been born in the Cove for nothing. My heart beat violently: I was a boy again. I knew that the preventive men were afoot, and the ancient instincts were still so powerful that I went forward almost at a run, intent upon communicating the news to any of the Cove people who might be interested. The village lies at the centre point of a semi- circular sweep of the coast. My advance haa been from the west at. first, and afterwards northerly, until I had arrived at the beginning of that long. I sweep. I could see the few lights still burning in the village, and some of the outlying houses were near enough for me to have hailed the occupiers had they stood in their doorways., It was here that the thing I am to tell you came to pass. A woman suddenly' appeared out of the darkness —some dip of the ground must have hidden her from my sight—and moved along the cliff, bearing , a lantern. As she advanced she swung it again I: and again, and I knew that she was giving the ; signal of safety to some boat that lay in the offing ! with a cargo of coneraband 'goods. I sprang forward, eager to warn her of what I had seen on the wastelands, but when I had come up with her I stood discomfited for a moment. ; The woman with the lantern was Sarah, and there was some change in her that made me speechless ir as I stood before her. I' had not spoke.' when she looked me in the face and was MI again, ' swaying the lantern. I sprang after her to warn ' her, but to my amazement she was nowhere visible. Perhaps, I thought, she had heard what I now , detected—the sound of voices drawing near; but I I still wondered that she had given no warning to ! the folk at sea before disappearing into a place of , safety. • I The voices ceased, and I advanced towards the village. The hour was somewhat late, for I had ; • loitered more than I thought; and the village was . asleep. It was only when I had come to its further -• end thai a man came running from the opposite direction. I recognised him despite the darkness. "Good evening, Anthony " I cried. He paused, hesitating. Then: "That Dick Trewollah, is it? " he cried. I "Iss," I said. ! "The wanderer's come back, 'then? Did 'ee take the road, or have 'ee eome by the cliffs? " j "I took the cliffs," 'I said. "'Twas good to ; tread on the heath again." "Did '.ee hear or see anything? " he asked. "There were more than me on the cliffs just now. I wondered if they were carriers or Revenue

div.head: PENKETH AND SANKEY.
div.p: PENKETH AND SANKEY.

EASTER SENDAY.—There were large congregations at the Easter Day services at Sankey Church when the Rev. J. R. Jones preached, taking for his text at the morning service " The Resurrection of the deed" and at the evening service " Ele\ is risen as He said unto you." The choir very tastefully rendered two anthems, viz.," King of Kings and Lord of Lords" and He is risen." At the close of the seivice Miss Standish played the "Hallelujah Chorus," the congregatt n standing.

HEATH•ROAD BOWLING CLUB.—The annual gather- ing of the members of the Heath-road Bowling Club took place on Easter Monday afternoon, when about 28 members sat down to a substantial knife and fork tea, which had been generously provided by Messrs. Jackson, Johnson, and Snoddy. Subsequently the annual meet- ing of the club was held, when the general business of the club was transacted, and confirmed. The follow- ing gentlemen who are members of the committee, viz., Messrs. Hughes, Moston, Randall, and Wood, offered prizes for competit'on during the current season. , Mr. and Mrs. James Dodds had been invited to the , gathering, and Mrs. Dodds with Miss Booth presided at the tea tables. Mr. Dodds was unanimously elected I president of the club for the ensuing twelve months. Mr. Dodds, in accepting the office, said he had ,been deeply touched by the kind words of the mover and seconder, and of the Rev. John Gunnell, who had supported anthput the proposition for his election. He felt that the establishment of a club such as theirs was worthy of the best support of all who desired to further a popular form of outdoor exercise apart from the associations of a public-house. Games were then indulged in until dusk.

div.head: Good Fnday Stabbing Affray
div.p: Good Fnday Stabbing Affray

At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, William Bibby, of Winwick-road, was charged with assaulting his brother, James Bibby, on Good Friday. —The charge was reduced frout„one of unlawful wounding. Mr. T. S. Steel, who prosecuted, stated that the rnosecutor, along with another broth*, resided in Winwick-road. Late on Friday night prisoner came to the house and commenced to gum A struggle ensued, and the prisoner aimed a blob, the prosecutor with a table knife, which glanced ovc his shoulder and inflicted a wound in his back abou an inch in length. Another wound was also inflicted on the wrist. While the prosecutor was away at the Infirmary the prisoner threatened to kill the other brother, John Bibby.—The magistfates sent the prisoner to gaol for two months and bound him over in sureties of PAO or in default six months' imprison- ment.

All the civilised world will THE mourn at the news of the EX-PREMIER, death of Si r HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN. For ' some months past it had been obvious that his strength had run its course and that the days of his public activity were over. The actual news of his passing away, although it does not come as a shock or surprise, will plunge the whole British nation into grief, and will produce world-wide sympathy with us in our sorrow. The late PRIME MINISTER was the great inter- national apostle of goodwill among the nations of the world, and both by precept and example did perhaps more than any statesman of modern times to cultivate that goodwill. He had small patience with those who see in every foreigner an enemy, and whose whole international policy is built upon principles of bravado and defiance. Sir HENRY was before all things a human statesman, who believed that, whatever . may be the case with Governments, the civilised peoples of the world desire nothing so much as to be allowed to live in peace and amity the one with the other. That was the keystone of his foreign policy, and with the assistance of his • MAJESTY the KING he had, during the brief period of his Premiership, built up a spirit , of confidence in British goodwill which will stand the world in good stead for many years to come. His simplicity, straightforwardness, and obvious desire to believe the best possible about his fellow-man, his lofty conception of the gospel of humanity, his striving after high purpose, and his continued efforts to embody his noble principles so far as possible, in the statecraft of his country, were an example to the world of which the results will be felt in the coming generations. "To seek peace and and ensue it was his guiding motto in our foreign relations, and his striving after under- standings with the Chancelleries of Europe was of the utmost use in the promotion of international peace. Notwithstanding the keen political war- fare in which Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BA.NNER- MAN was in his later years constantly engaged, his loss will be sincerely mourned even by his opponents. It is a striking feature of our British public life that political differences do not gener- ally interfere with good personal relationships ; arid our late PRIME MINISTER was the living embodiment of that fine principle which does so much to keep our public institutions pure and wholesome. There were many times when he felt it necessary to criticise very severely the conduct of the nation's business by those who sat opposite him in the last Parliament ; but throughout all those dark days there were none who knew him intimately who had any syrnp ithy with the wild I and whirling aczusations of traitorous conduct which were made by irresponsible speakers from a thousand platforms. Sir HENRY lived to see the nation come round to his view. Indeed, probably the real secret of the hold he had upon the affections of the people was that his courage never failed him in the darkest hour. When it Was, difficult and almost dangerous to stand up for his principles, when the vast majority of the I nation were against him, when he was yelled at as a "Little Eaglander " and a "friend of every country but his own," when it would have been much easier for him to float with the tide of popular opinion than to fight against it, he never flinched.To him was entrusted the task of preserving the fair name of Britain's humanity and her traditional policy of protecting small and independent States, and although,once we were at war in South Africa, he never refused to vote the supplies for carrying it on, yet he did feel it incumbent upon him to protest against some of the methods which were being used in its prose- ution. div.head: ail 25, 1908.
div.p: war; and although at the time the nation was overwhelmingly against him, ,it eventually came to see that he had been right all the time. The grant of self-government to the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony within a few years of the war was a triumph of the principles always advo- cated by Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN, and at the same time a wonderful object lesson to all the peoples of the world. To us of the Liberal Party the death of this distinguished statesman is a very severe blow. No Prime Minister of our generation was ever so popular with the Members of the House of Commons, and no man was ever more successful in keeping the various elements which must always be found in the Liberal Party, if it is to be really Liberal, in good understanding the one with the other. All respected his sincerity, all had faith in his sound instinct and judgment. He was not masterful like Gladstone or a brilliant orator like Rosebery. He was a plain, simple, industrious man, with a profound belief in democratic principles which he applied to every problem which faced him in his great office. He took the Leadership of the Liberal Party at a time when it was forsaken by some of those who ought to have been its best friends, and by his straight forward and manly courage in refusing to be a time-server, or to sacrifice the great guiding prin- ciples which be believed, and rightly believed, had made Britain a leader among the nations of the world, he led his party to the greatest triumph in the history of politics. He knew that the heart of his countrymen was right, and was content to wait for the vindication of his principles. His success was a striking lesson in the value of steadfastness in political faith. Short• sighted politicians, not so very many years ago, were scorning the possibility of Sir HENRY CAMPBELL-BANE ERMAN ever becoming First Minister of the Crown ; but when the country had got over the war fever, and desired to settle down to the cultivation of the arts of peacqthey with one accord felt that there was but one man to carry out their desires. The personal affection and regard which the deceased statesman had inspired among his followers was a party asset of priceless value. Now that, after a brief retire- ment, he has passed "beyond these voices," the sympathy of the world will be sincere, the regret of the nation will be great, and the grief of the Liberal Party will be not less deep even than that which followed his illustrious predecessor to his grave.

The abject failure of the THE FORGED now notorious forged ticket TICKET TRICK, trick in connection with the recent Parr Hall demon- stration in favour of the Licensing Bill still appears to rankle in the minds of those who had best say least about it. Our friend the"Observer,"for instance cannot keep off the topic. A fortnight ago it referred loftily to "alleged forged or bogus tickets" —as if there was a doubt even as to their existence. Last week it remarked in the same strain "Many people are wondering why the meeting in Parr Hall should have been a ticket meeting. It has been said that spurious tickets had been issued," etc. The " Observer " " doth protest too much 1" If it cared to be ' candid and honest we dare say it 'could give its readers some exact and really interesting information about the forged tickets. Their origin should be pretty well known in the ranks of the Conservative and Liquor Joint Party. We might add that the Citizens' Temperance League, as promoters of the meeting in ques- tion, have been patiently waiting for the leaders of the opposite party or parties to dissociate themselves from such discreditable tactics as the forging of tickets for a public meeting. It was thought that gentlemen like Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. W. P. Rylands, Mr. John White, and Councillor Fulton-Smith would have been eager to avow themselves ignorant of the forged ticket trick and to express their disgust at such a breach of party-political etiquette, but all have remained strangely silent to this day. Meanwhile the" Observer ' tries, with a faithful- ness worthy of a better cause, to further the idea that the forged tickets were a figment of someone's imagination. The sceptics might apply to the Chief Constable,who personally collected a huge pocketful at the door of the Hall.

The President of the War- A CALL To Ants. rington Liberal Association Mr. C. E. Parker J.P., has issued a circular letter to the members Parker, takes the direct form of a call to arms in the battle for the Government Licensing Bill. The Liberal Party 'in the town has already been actively associated with others in the fight for Temperance, but the members of the Association have not, as a body ' identified themselves with the struggle and it is Mr. Parker's aim to rally them for the front rank in this memorable conflict. In his forceful and convincing epistle he emphasizes the fact that "The Trade has become so linked with the Conservative Party that it seems to have adeed their political associa- tion to its tied-house system." He then quotes the words of the Executive of the National Trade Defence Fund avowing its purpose of securing " the return to the House of Commons and other elected bodies of candidates favourable to Trade interests." It cannot be doubted for a moment that in Warrington at any rate this is the common aim of the Trade and the Tory party. Their unity of purpose was apparent long before the new Licensing Bill clinched matters, and even the November elections were overshadowed by the menace of their sinister alliance. Since then the Trade has slipped into the mire and dragged the Tory Party with it. Liberals know where to find the foe, fortunately, and we believe they will welcome their President's strong lead at this critical junc- ture. The health, the morality,and the prosperity of the town and country are alike threatened, and while Liberals aro ever ready to fight the heredi- tary foe they must be prepared to exert exceptional effort now the, that foe is working hand and glove with the most powerful and unscrupulous monopoly in the country. The opening skirmish , has already given them an advantage which must be pushed home in. order to break once and finally the power of the baneful traffice which aims at corrupting all branches of public administra- tion for its own selfish ends.
Mr. Bryce, who cannot ordinarily be considered an
POPULAR
GOVERNMENT.
upholder-of the conservative

tendency in politics, has just delivered a remarkable speech upon the attitude of men of genius and of educational intelligence towards politics which cannot fail to arrest the attention of students on all sidss in this country. The British Ambassador at Wash- ington is a discerning student of modern as well as of ancient history, and he declares that throughout the continent of Europe to-day distinguished men are more generally conservative in temper and less heartily democratic 1/3 opinion than men of the Isame type were in 1858. His explanation of Ws fact is that in the middle of last century arbitrary government prevailed on the Continent, except in a few small countries. Since then arbitrary government has given way to popular government to a very large degree. While arbitrary government held the field, the superior minds, seeing the evils that existed under it, were strongly liberal. But the advatice of democracy has changed the position. Popular government in experience has proved productive of certain evils of its own, and the superior minds recognising these have turned away from the faith to which they would naturally have allied them- selves were arbitrary government still in vogue. An additional reason which he gives is that they are influenced by demands made in the name of iberty for further changes which are deemed

dangerous. Mr. Bryce is a shrewd and experienced observer, and the tendencies to which he refers undoubtedly exist. But there are obvious limita- tions to argument upon these lines. In politics action and re-action are recognised consequences ; but the progress of one generation is seldom, if ever, reversed by that succeeding. The tendency to-day may be, probably is, towards caution. Great minds are often curiously timid, and democracy has of recent years demonstrated forces which are calculated to increase timidity. But the ideal of popular government will not be affected because the leading minds are inclined to " mark time," and to turn their attention to estimating the consequences of further advance, and devising barriers for directing the flow of progress and preventing it from breaking the bounds of safety. No one who knows Mr. Bryce can imagine that he meant to convey that the superior intellects were turning back to the old order which the erilightment of the nineteenth century banished. Popular government is estab- lished today ; its extension will no doubt be more gradual in the future than it has been in the last fifty years ; but it is none the less assured.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
One of Mr. Jopason-Hicks' Committee Booms in Manchester,which is established in a shop, bears on its windows these mixed placards :
TO BE LET OR SOLD. JOYNSON-HICSS Tms TIME.
This can scarce be called a judicious backing of your- self. _ _

The " Observer " says of the recent Parr Hall meetings on the Licensing Bill :—" There was no comparison between the two meetings—the one of protest and the one of support." We quite agree. The meeting addressed by the Bishop of Liverpool in support of the Bill was the largest and most enthusiastic gathering ever held in Warrington. It practically flattened out the disciples of the " x x x."

Lancashire people will lce pleased to learn that Mr. John Morley will on his accession to the peerage take his title from a town in his native county, and will become Lord Morley of Lytham. Mr_ Morley's mother is buried in the churchyard of St. Cuthbert in this seaside town. His election to the office of Chancellor of the Manchester University will, however, occur probably before he has assumed his new title, while he is still—Mr. John Morley. * * * An Anfield schoolboy was required to write a short essay on " Wild Animals." This is bow he began : —" Wild animals formerly roamed at large in this country, which was infested with wolves, but to-day wild animals are only to be found in England enclosed in theological gardens." It may be that here there was an unconscious allusion to the education controversy.

* * * A working man's wife sends to the press the follow- ing, which shows that she, at least, believes that reduced facilities will lead to decreased drinking : " Dear sir,— Could you plese arange to shut public house every morning until eight o'clock, to let my man get to his work sober? He won't have is break- fast with me if he can get is drop at public house. And plese shut them up at eight at night on Saturday,to make my man come home erly." * * *

The brewers seem to have become very humbled in spirit, and there is no doubt that the tide has turned against them on the Licensing Bill. They have held no meetings in Warrington this week, and there is nothing fresher on the walls than the big glass and the little glass, and one seems as stale as the other, We are informed that the real meaning of the disparity in size between the two glasses is this : The little one indicates how much beer there is in the large one when the froth has been blown off. * * * Said Joynson to Hicks: " We're in a nice fix, Thanks to you with your Stupid Protectionist tricks." Said Hicks unto Joynson : "Your wrong. Can't you see If they don't vote for you They may vote for me ? "

• 0 .- A few days ago many passers-by were greatly surprised to find posted outside the entrance gate of the Brownlow-hill Workhouse, Liverpool, a placard declaring that if the Licensing Bill now before the country should become law "this establishment will ' have to be closed." There was a certain grim humour about the announcement, which, however, failed to appeal to the workhouse officials, who unceremoniously tore down the poster as soon as they discovered it. The explanation of the affair is that a practical joker had obtained the placard from a public-house in the neighbourhood and had slyly attached it to the work- house gates. .
It is hard upon the poor widow who was completely ruined by the Chinese labour policy of the Govern- ment to have to go again through the same trouble in consequence of the Licensing Bill.

* Dr. T. J. Macnamara M.P.,Secretary to the Admiralty, said at Newcastle on Thursday night that he had not a shadow of doubt that "the Licensing Bill would pass both Houses of Parliament before the close of the present year of grace."

* * * For the first time during the contest Mrs. Cornwallis West was persuaded to speak on her son's behalf on Thursday afternoon. Addressing a meeting at Slande- hill she said : " I will just say that whilst I heard a good deal about dear coal and dear beer, my motto is Vote for dear Winston." * * * First-class cricket began on Monday. It is easy to write the sentence, bat nobody who did not play or look on can gauge the amount of tragedy the few words can conceal. The situation of a fieldsman (says the "Evening Standard ") when snow is appearing at fitful intervals and threatening all the time is much worse than penal servitude; and we can easily understand that men who were subjected to the torture thought enviously of the lucky fellows wheeling harrows at Portland. A batsman was a happy man, especially when he was hitting. A. bowler, though he might be discovering extra- ordinary difficulty in holding and hurling the ball, was also able to keep himself compara- tively warm. But the others, shivering under an extra supply of heavy sweaters and endeavouring to keep their fingers from being frost-bitten, were in a state to arouse sympathy from every beholder. But alas ! every beholder was in a position where all his sym- pathy was needed jor himself. If anything he was worse off than the players. They were in flannels ; he might be in furs ; but they did not get a chance of good healthy running exercise between the overs, whereas he was condemned by his enthusiasm to sit still and wondered how long cricket would survive such weather. Everybody must have come to the conclusion that cricket in the winter is a grave mistake

Warrington Musical Festival. The first Warrington Musical Festival is to be held at the Parr Hall on May 23rd, and judging by the enthusiasm which is being manifested success should be assured. Some famous choirs are expected to compete, and the programme will be one calculated to delight all music lovers. Intending competitors should bear in mind that to-day (Saturday) is the last day for the receipt of entries. All information will be gladly supplied by the Secretary, Mr. R. W. Cook, Froghall-lane. "The Mandarin." Successful performances of this comic opera were given by St. Paul's Choir and friends in the girls' echool, Kendrick-street, on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday evenings. Notwithstanding the limitations imposed by the small stage accommodation, a very creditable representation of a delightful opera was given and afforded much pleasure to fairly large audiences. The performers thdroughly entered into the spirit of the work and their acting was charac- terised by an abandon and vivacity which made it most acceptable. The voices ot the well-balanced chorus, too, blended nicely, while the soloists did full justice to their numbers. All the leading parts were in capable hands and the performances went With a splendid swing from beginning to end. The following is a list of the characters :—The Mandarin, Mr. E. Walker; Yung-Shi (The Mandarin's Daughter), Mrs. Wilson ; So-Fah, Miss Lawless, Doh-Ray-Me, Miss Cox, (Chinese young ladies) ; Chang (Public Prosecutor), Mr. C. Geldard ; Chung (Counsel for defence), Mr. Cr. Radcliffe ; Usher, Mr. W. Richard- son ; Foreman of Jury, Mr. J. Morris ; Sing-Song, Miss Gardner; Lieutenant John Smith,Mr. W. Tynan; Colonel Coldsteel, Mr. P. Smith; Captain Bluff (Of the Royal Navy), Mr. A. Cottrell. A feature of the Feast of Lanterns in the second act was:a clever conjuring entertainment by Mr. A. Lloyd. Praise is due to Mr. E. Wilkes (conductor). Mr. R. Lonsdale (stage manager), and Mr. J. Killip (assistant stage manager.) ASHLBY'S, New Address 4, Buttermarket Street.—Advt The Assessment of an Off-Licence. A meeting of the Warrington Assessment Committee Was held in the Board room at the Workhouse yesterday, Mr. J. Billinge presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. W. Houghton, E. L. Bent, W. Gill, E. J. Sutton (acting assistant clerk), R. R. Meacock (valuer), and W. H. Woodcock (assistant overseer).— Owing to a difficulty in forming a quorum, the coin- mencement of the proceedings was delayed forty minutes beyond the usual time.—Mr. T. S. Steel appealed on behalf of Lewis Edward Jowett against the assessment of an off-licence, 1, Rolleston.street, Which stood at £42 gross and £36 rateable.—Mr. Steel said that unfortunately since notice of appeal had been given the rates had gone up consideeably but he hoped that would not prejudice the position of his client. Mr. Jowett was a tenant of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Limited. He took the premises some six months ago and the rental at that time was £36 per year. After he had been there a short time he found it was totally im- possible to carry on the business at a profit and he saw Messrs. Walker in Liverpool and told them that he thought the business was going to keep him but be Sound it was impossible. He was a wire drawer and he had to return to his work at Messrs. Rylande Bros. After some consideration the firm said that it was impossible for Mr. Jewett to make ends meet with a rental of £36 and reduced it to £24. Even at £24 be Was unable to make a livelihood. He was not selling more than 21 barrels per week on an average. If the licence were taken from the house he submitted the rental would not amount to £24 —lt was decided to reduce the assessment to £36 gross and £3O 108. rateable —Mr. Woodcock submitted the new valuation list for the borough of Warrington. The gross value was £349,774 and rateable £279,226, an increase on the half-year of £20,225 10s. gross and £13,499 rateable; and an increase on the year of £23,710 gross and 416,401 rateable. The figures were larger than usual in consequence of the valuer having re-assessed several Works in the town and considerably increased them.— As this was the last meeting of the committee for the Present financial year Mr. Houghton moved a vote of thanks to the chairman and vice-chairman (Mr. Jolley and Mr. Billinge). He remarked that no-one could have presided over the meetings with more credit than Mr. Jolley and he had been ably seconded by Mr. Mr. Billinge. —Mr Bent seconded and said he felt no member could fill the position of Chairman so effici- ently as Mr. Jolley.--Mr. Gill supported and the vote was heartily accorded. For influenza Coughs take Woods' Great Peppermint Cure' I/11 and 2/9.—Advt.

div.head: DEWSBURY POLL. Mr. Walter Runciman
div.p: THE DEWSBURY POLL. Mr. Walter Runciman

The election in the Parliamentary borough of Dews- bury, rendered necessary by Mr. Walter Runciman's recceptance of the post of President of the Board of Education, took place on Thursday. Mr. Runciman's ze-elcction was opposed by Mr. W. B. Boyd-Carpenter, Conservative, and Mr. Ben Turner, Labour. The result Was declared last night as follows: Mr. Runciman (L) Mr. Boyd-Carpenter (C) 4,078 Mr. Ben Turner (Lab.) L majority over C L majority over Lab. C majority over Lab. There was it will be seen. a smaller poll than at the general election, although the number of voters on the l'egister had increased from 13,951 to 14,054. At Dewsbury, as in other constituencies, the Liberal Vote and the Liberal majority rose in 1905 to an < abnormal height. In straight fights between Liberal t end Tory the Liberal majority at Dewsbury has varied 'between 2,089 (in 1892) and 2,460 (in 1885). The elec- tion preceding that of 1906—the bye-election of 1902, at vilich Mr. Runciman was first returned for the boroutgh—was a three-cornered fight, and the Liberal Lciajonty over the Conservative was only 1,157, as corn- Pared with 1,516 on Thursday. The Conservative vote ~_.‘vaa between 400 and 500 larger in 1902 than it was on itursday, the Socialist vote was less by 850, and the Liberal vote was nearly the same. PREVIOUS ELECTIONS. div.head: NORTH-WEST MANCHESTER ELECTION.
div.p: NORTH-WEST MANCHESTER ELECTION.
MR. CHURCHILL NARROWLY DEFEATED.

Polling took place yesterday in the North-West Division of Manchester after one of the most memor_ able by-election contests which has ever taken place The morning opened with a snow-storm but after about an hour's downfall the weather cleared. and the conditions for the rest of the day were all that could be desired. _

Excitement in the city was intense throughout the day, and the display of party favours was prodigious. Motor-cars hummed about the division in hundreds, and there was everywhere a display of election enthusiasm such as Manchester has never before experienced. '

THE RESULT. The result was declared from the Town Hall at 9.30 p.m. as follows : Mr. W. JOYNSON-HICKS (U) 5,417 Mr. WINSTON CHURCHILL (L) Mr. DAN IRVING (Social Democrat) 276 Majority 429 FORMER ELECTIONS. 1906. Mr. W. S. Churchill (L) 5,639 Mr. W. Joynson-Hicks (C) 4,398
Liberal majority 1895. Sir W. H. Houldsworth (C) Mr. T. F. Byrne (L) 3,526 Conservative majority In 1892, and again in 1900, Sir William Houldsworth was returned unopposed. •

div.head: BOLTON SCHOOL.
div.p: THE BOLTON SCHOOL.

div.head: VISIT OF INSPECTION.
div.p: A VISIT OF INSPECTION.

Yesterday afternoon the members of the Sites and Buildings sub-Committee of the Education Committee inspected the Bolton Council School at Latchford prior to it being taken over from the contractor. There were present the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst), Aldermen Bolton : - (chairman of the Committee), Bennett, Pierpoint, Tinnion, Councillors Fulton Smith, (chairman of the Education Committee), Pemberton, Lord, Evans, Messrs. R. T. Fairclough, G. Walker, J. Moore Murray (secretary and director), R. B. Roberts (assistant director), T. Longdin (borough surveyor), J. Fairhurst (borough treasurer), A. T. Hallaway (deputy town clerk), R. Garnett and S. Wright (archi- tects), Harry Fairclough (contractor), and H. Hallard (clerk of works.) The date of the opening of the school has not yet been fixed, but in all probability it will be in the second or third week in May. Last evening Alderman Bolton (chairman of the Sites and Buildings Committee) entertained the mem- bers of that Committee and other members of the Education Committee and Town Council at dinner at the Town Hall. DESCRIPTION OF THE BUILDING.

The " Bolton " Council School, which has been recently erected adjacent to Lower Walsh-lane, Latch- ford, and facing the new street, Longdin-street, is now practically completed, and it is anticipated that it will be ready for the attendance of scholars within a fort- night. The site is an admirable one, with large play- ground space, a portion of which—on the West and South boundaries—is laid out as gardens for " Nature study." The latter, which is 35 feet wide and runs co-extensive with the present buildings, is expected to form a pleasing feature along Longdin-street. As there were several large healthy trees on the site it was thought desirable to preserve them and the same will remain, with iron guards placed round for protection. The school consists of two departments, infants' on the ground floor and girls on the first floor. Each department is arranged for 360 scholars,and divided into 7 class-rooms. The class-rooms open into the Lateral Halls, and are all under full supervision from same. The playgrounds are in full view of the teachers' rooms, and the latter, being adjacent to cloak-rooms, entrances, and staircases, have complete control over same. The class-rooms and Lateral Hall are well lighted, lofty and airy rooms, and are heated and venti- lated on the most modern lines. The external design of the buildings is, of necessity, simple in character, and throughout the structure there is absence of any extravagance. The outside facings are of grey St. Helens bricks relieved by red pressed brick base and terracotta dressings. The caretaker's house is situated on the North side of the playgrounds, with ample accommodation for the occupant, and the position is such that when the future boys' school is built the house will be centrally placed and convenient for access to the several departments. The premises have been erected from the designs of Messrs. J. E. Wright, Garnett and Wright, architects, &c.. War- rington, by M. Harry Fairclough, and the work has been executed in a most skilful manner. Mr. H. Hallard has acted as clerk of works for the Education Committee. Special contracts have been executed by the following Arms :—Grates ,mantels, Btc., Mr. H. frairclough, Warrington; tiled dadoes, Mr. H. Fairclough, Warrington; boundary railings, itc., Mr, J. S. Garland, Warrington ; electric lighting, Ste. Messrs. Haggett and Worthington, Warrington ; beat- ing, Messrs. Dinning and Cooke, Newcastle-on-Tyne ; ventilating, The Sun Ventilating Co.,Glasgow; sanitary fittings, Messrs. Morrison, Ingram and Co., Manchester; cloak fittings, Mr. W. F. Spencer, Oldham; hoist,Messrs. C. Whittaker, and Co., Bradford ; glazed screen and demonstration table, Mr. John Heywood, Manchester ; door and window furniture, Messrs. W. and R.Leggott, Bradford ; paving playgrounds, Messrs. A. Walker and Sons, Leeds.

Lawrence—Birchall.

There was a pretty wedding at the Warrington Parish Church on Thursday when Mr. Edward Law- rencelsecond son of the late Mr. Edward Lawrence, of Warrington, was married to Miss Maud Hilda Birchen, second daughter of Mr. Joseph Birchall, 131, Bridge- street. A large congregation witnessed the ceremony the Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) officiating. Mr. F. M. Darby, Mus. Bac. presided at the organ and played festal selections including Mendelssohn's " Wedding March." The bride, who was given away by her lather, was belutifully gowned in white silk trimmed with lace, with hat to match, and carried a lovely bouquet of roses and lilies of the valley. Her ornament was a gold pendant, set with pearls and rubies, the gift of the bridegroom She was attended by three brides- maids —Misses Amy Florence Birchall and Elsie Gertrude Birchall (sisters of the bride) and Miss Lily Lawrence (sister of the bridegroom) who were prettily attired in mauve silk crystoline trimmed with mauve velvet, and champagne coloured hats trimmed with mauve. Their bouquets were composed of tulips and roses and they wore gold pendants, the gifts of the bridegroom. Ur. Harry Lawrence (brother of the bridegroom) discharged the duties of best man. As the bridal party left the church, the bells rang out a joyous peal. After the ceremony, a reception was held at the house of the bride's parents, about forty- six guests attending. Later in the day the happy couple departed for London, where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was of green cloth, with hat to match.
