div.head: LOCAL WEDDINGS. Bradfori7—T3owcock.
div.p: LOCAL WEDDINGS. Bradfori7—T3owcock.

In the presence of a large congregation the marriage was solemnized at Holy Trinity Church on Thursday afternoon of Mr. Karl Bradford, only son of Mrs. McGregor, Weaverham, and Miss Florence Bowcock, 133, Liverpool-road. The Vicar (Rev. E. C. E. Carleton) officiated. The bride, who was given away ;by her father, looked charming in a cream cloth princess robe trimmed with violet net, with hat to match. She carried a lovely bouquet of lilies and white violets. The bridesmaids were Miss Annie Bowcock (sister of the bride), and Miss Nellie McGregor (niece of the bridegroom), who were tastefully attired in pale blue cloth trimmed with net, with hats to match. Their bouquets were composed of daffodils. Mr. Charles Houghton acted as best men. Mr. W. B. Randall was at the organ and as the bridal party left the church he played Mendelssohn's " Wedd- ing March." After the ceremony a reception was held at 133, Liverpool-road, about sixty guests being present. Later the happy couple left for Derbyshire where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride's travelling dress was a heliotrope costume, with hat to match. Many handsome presents were received.

Itioxon—Rowson. On Wednesday, the marriage of the Reverend Reginald Stewart Mc:mon, M.A., 8.D., Senior Classical Master of King's School, Canterbury, elder son of Mr. George Mozon, of Colwyn, North Wales, to Miss Ina Mary Rowson, daughter of the late Mr. Richard Whitlock Rowson of Warrington, was solemnized at St. Anne's Church, Soho, W. The service which was ally choral was conducted by the Reverend J. H. Cardwell, rector of the parish, assisted by the Rev. Dr. Nairn, headmaster of Merchant Taylors' School, brother-in-law of the bridegroom, who also gave an address. The bride was given away by her brother, Mr. L. R. Rowson, and the Rev. T. A. Moson, vicar of Alfreton, Derbyshire, brother of the bridegroom, performed the duties of best man. The bride wore a gown of white satin oriental,trimmed with Tambour lace and Brussels net with satin train draped from the shoulders, and over a wreath of orange blossom, myrtle and heather, her mother's handsomely embroidered Brussels net veil. She wore a beautiful necklace, the gift of the bridegroom. The bridesmaids were Miss Doris Ruth Rowson, sister of the bride, and Miss Sylvia Jocelyn Nairn, niece of the bridegroom. The former was dressed in an Empire gown of pale green Liberty satin, trimmed with silver galon, with silver shoes and stockings, and a picture hat in drawn green chiffon, trimmed with silver and moss roses. Miss Sylvia Jocelyn Nairn wore a white embroidered lawn dress over pale green silk with a white mushroom Liberty hat in drawn -.white crepe tied with green strings. Tney wore pretty pearl brooches, their gifts from the bridegroom, and carried tiny bouquets of tea roses. The duties of page were most successfully carried out by Master Ronald Atkin, cousin of the bride, dressed in a white sailor suit. As the wedding was a very quiet one, only near relatives were present. For travelling the bride wore a leather coloured box cloth costume and hat en suite.

div.head: Markham—Baine.
div.p: Markham—Baine.

At St. Stephen's Church, Gloucester-road, London, on Thursday afternoon, the marriage took place of the Rev. Algernon A. Markham, vicar of Grimsby, and formerly of St. Jude's, West Derby, Liverpool (at one time curate of the Warrington Parish Church), youngest son of the Rev. C. W. Markham, and Miss Winifred Edith Baine, younger daughter of Lady Constance Baine. of Mill House, Belstead, Ipswich,and niece of the Marquis of Hertford, of Ragley Hall, Alcester, Warwickshire. The service was fully choral, and the ceremony was conducted by the Rev. Lord Victor Seymour, vicar of St. Stephen's Church, and uncle of the bride, assisted by the Rev. Roger Markham, brother of the bridegroom. The bride was given away by her father, Captain Miles Baine, and Mr. Richard Pearson acted as best man. The reception, held at the vicarage of St. Stephen's Church, 78, Cornwall-gardens, kindly lent by the Rev. Lord and Lady Victor Seymour (uncle and aunt of the bride), Was largely attended, among those invited being Colonel Markham, Captain Miles Baine, Lady Florence Blunt, Mr. and Lady Horatio Erskine, Captain and Mrs. Philip Baine, Lieut.- Colonel and Lady Georgina Horne Drummond, Lord and Lady William Seymour, Lord Ernest Seymour, the Marquis and Marchioness of Hertford, Lady Knightley of Fansley, Miss Baine, Lieutenant M. Baine, RN., the Rev. Roger and Mrs. Markham, Mr. and Mrs. Warren Markham, &c. In the afternoon the Rev. Algernon and Mrs. Mark- ham left for Tansley Pau, en route for the Italian lakes, where they will spend their honeymoon. The presents were numerous and costly, and among ,the givers were the Marquis and Marchioness of Hertford, Lord and Lady William Seymour, Lord and Lady Victor Seymour, Lady Florence Blunt, Lord Ernest Seymour, Lady Knightley of Fansley, Lieut-Colonel and Lady G-eorgina Horne Drummond, the congrega- tion of St. Jude's, West Derby, Liverpool, &c.

Turner—Evans. A pretty wedding and one which aroused consider- able interest took place at St. Barnabas' Church on Tuesday afternoon,wlaen Mr. William Turner, assistant ,maaLer at St. Barnabas' day school and youngest son of Mr. James Turner, was married to Miss Elsie Alice Evans, second daughter of Mr. Thomas Evans, Folly- lane, organist at St. Barnabas' Church. The bride and bridegroom are well-known in the parish and a crowded congregation assembled to witness the cere- mony. The officiating clergy were the Rev. J. H G. Hollingworth and the Rev. J. W. Glendenning. The service was choral, the members of Mr. Turner's class, in addition to the choir boys, being in attendance and leading the singing of the hymns "0 perfect love "and " The King of Love my Stiepherd is "and Psalm cxxviii. Mr. T. G. Reeves presided at the organ and played appropriate selections, including the "Bridal March" from "Lobengrin" and Mendelssohn's "Wedding March." The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in stone-coloured silk poplin trimmed with ivory silk. She wore a cream crinoline hat with ostrich plume and orange blossom, and carried a lovely bouquet of Easter lilies, roses, lilies of the 'valley, maidenhair fern and smilax. The bridesmaids were the Misses Cissie Evans and Eva Evans (sisters of the bride), Eva Sherratt, Mabel Turner and Isabel Ward (nieces of the bridegroom ) The Mi4ies Evans were , tastefully gowned in fawn voile trimmed with ivory silk and lace, with green crinoline hats trimmed with flowers and foliage. .Their bouquets were composed of tulips, lilies of the valley and maidenhaie fern. The other little bridesmaids were prettily dressed in white with white silk bonnets and carried bouquets of marguerites and tulips. Mr. T. Evans, jun. (brother of the bride) discharged the duties of best man. After the wedding a reception and social were held in St. Barnabas' school, about seventy guests being present. The newly married couple were the recipients of many handsome presents, including a Kidderminster rug from the scholars of St. Barnabas' school and a mahogany cabinet from the teachers. Richmond --Dickenson.

An interesting wedding took place at St. Paul's Church, on Thursday afternoon, the bridegroom being Mr. Herbert Richmond, eldest son of Ur. John Richmond, 11, Alfred street, Stockton Heath and the bride Miss Ellen Dickenson, second daughter of Councillor James Dickenson, 97, Bewsey-road. There was a large congregation, the service being conducted by the Rev. W. Bracecamp. The bride, who was given away by her father, was charmingly attired in a silver grey silk voile dress, and leghoru hat with ostrich feather, anid carried a bouquet of orchids. She was attended by four bridesmaids: —Misses Alice, Emily, Gertrude and Eva Dickenson (sisters of the bride), and Miss Olive Poppitt, of Manchester. The Misses Alice and Emily Dickenson wore pretty dresses of pink silk voile, with hats to match, and the other little bridesmaids were attired in white silk trimmed with pink. They carried bouquets of tulips and white and pink carnations. Mr. James Richmond (brother of the bridegroom) discharged the duties of best man and Mr. Ernest Llewellyn, of Manchester, acted as groomsman. After the ceremony a reception was held in Providence schoolroom, Stockton Heath, over 100 guests attending. The honeymoon is being spent at Blackpool. The following is a list of the presents : Bridegroom to bride, watch studded with pearls, and iress ring. div.head: Union Clerkship.
div.p: Union Clerkship.

Sir,—l observe that on the consideration of this appointment at last Wednesday's meeting of the Guardians, Mr. A. Brooks is reported as having said : "Mr. NV. C. Brooks who moved the resolution at the committee meeting made several statements and I take it that those who voted with him voted on those state- ments. When you come to analyse them they are absolutely incorrect. I will take one gentleman who has served seventeen years. If at the end of live years he became incapacitated yon would have to pay him £l5O Os. Bd. If you take a man who has no service you pay him nothing. At the end of ten years the man with seventeen years' previous service would on becom- ing incapacitated receive £lB4 10s., and the man with no previous service would get LOS 6s. Bd. und so on. That is sufficient to show that the vote was taken on statements which were quite erroneous." As I was the only condidate who had served 17 years as an Assistant Clerk I take it that Mr. A. Brooks' remarks specially applied to me, and as it appears that such remarks were evidently made under a wrong impression, I, in fairness to those Guardians who, knowinr, me and my qualifications, so kindly supported my application, take this opportunity of correcting such statements so far as they apply to myself. First, I stated in the printed form of application, in a paragraph specially allotted for the purpose, that I had no previous service which would count for super- annuation, not having been appointed Assistant Clerk by I the Guardians (in my case the Clerks had to appoint I their own assistants); and second, Mr. A. Brooks' state- runt that" if you take a man who has no service you pay him nothing" though referring to another (but not selected) candidate equally applied to myself. It is to be regretted that the statements of Mr. A. Brooks—as far as they applied to me—should have been allowed to pass without contradiction, as I cannot help but think that some of those Guardians who wished to study the interests of the ratepayers refrained from giving me their vote.— Yours faithfully, C. COLE. Earlestown, 22nd April, 1903. •

div.head: THEFT FROM A WORKS. -- Man Breaks His Leg.
div.p: THEFT FROM A WORKS. -- Man Breaks His Leg.

At the Borough Police Court on Thursday before Messrs. John Fairclough (in the chair), Charles White and F. W. Monks, Harry Ditchfield, Victoria-street,was charged with stealing 74 lbs. of scrap copper wire, value 375. from Messrs. Greenings works on Monday. He pleaded guilty. Mr. E. Draper,who prosecuted on behalf of the firm, said that at 12.15 on Monday, two men were seen on the wall of the works. They were seen to lower a sack containing something which seemed to be heavy. One man fell from the wall and injured himself and was taken to the Infirmary where he was detained with a broken leg. The other man (the prisoner) was seen to run away by the lodgeman but was subsequently arrested. It was a most bare- faced theft. The railway embankment had been examined and marks were found which showed that the men had gained admission to the works by means of climbing over the wall. Thefts from large works were very prevalent but in many Cases the thieves had not been captured, so he asked the magis- trates to deal severely with that case and inflict such punishment as would act as a deterrant to others. Prisoner: lam very sorry. I have a crippled wife and three children to look after. Mr. Monks : You should have thought of that before. How much money did you earn? Prisoner : .t 1 a week. .

The Rev. Leonard .1. Rich, vicar, presided at the vestry meeting for St. Thomas's Churcti, St. Helens, on Easter Monday morning.—Mr. Rich said there was not. very much to report on the past year, which had been very happy and harmonious. He asked the vestry, as a first duty to pass a vote of sympathy with the mother and family ot Mr. Oliver Heslop, one of their sidesmen, who died after a serious illness during his year of office, and this was accordingly done. Mr. Critchley was re-appointed vicar's warden, and Mr. Thomas Mallatrat people's warden. The following sidesmen were appointed :—Messrs. John Lewis, R. H. Bowles, R. Ford, J. Forber, A. Caldwell, Peter Taylor, E. J. J nhes, J. Pnthian, J. W. Warr, J. Anders, C. W. Rippon, and A. J. Tickle. Messrs. W. Porter and H. Telford were re-appointed ruri.decanal representatives. The Vicar said he was pleased to state that the num- ber of communicants on Easter Day was larger than ever—viz., 512. The offertories had increased, but there had been a good deal of expenditure on repairs and renewals, which left them with a debit balance of £lO 14s. The freewill offering had not suffered by reason of the increased collections, but was £4B is. 3d. more than last year. There was a balance of £852 Bs. Od- in hand on the fund for the restoration of the church. Votes of thanks closed the meeting.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
THE WIDOW'S PIG.

At Runcorn, on Tuesday, Catherine Osborne, a widow, pleaded guilty to not keeping isolated a pig she had purchased. The woman said she did not know she should not let the pig mix with the others.—Mr. Ockle- stone said it was a very serious offence, but the magis- trates would deal leniently with her, and order her to pay £l.

div.head: BISHOP AND LICENSING.
div.p: BISHOP AND LICENSING.

At the vestry meeting of St. Paul's Church, Widnes, on Tuesday, Mr. Thomas Hewitt moved the following resolution :—" That this meeting, representing the parishioners of St. Paul's Church, desires to acknow- ledge with gratitude and admiration the noble stand taken by the Lord Bishop of Liverpool in the cause of temperance, and trusts that God may bless his efforts in the cause of national sobriety and righteousness." After a short discussion the resolution was defeated by a large majority.

div.head: BRUTAL HUSBAND AND FORGIVING MFR.
div.p: BRUTAL HUSBAND AND FORGIVING MFR.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, John Owen Rees, of South-road, Weston Point, was charged with unlawfully wounding his wife, Ellen, at midnight, on Saturday, by striking her on the head with a poker. Mr. Lake, who defended, said whatever happened was the result of the wife's temper. She admitted that she was to blame, and did not now desire to prosecute. He was a man of unblemished character.

The Bench reduced the charge to one of common assault, and Mrs. Rees went into the box and said she had been married for thirty years and had a family of nine. She was to blame, and did not remember exactly what took place. She did not wish to prosecute. The doctor attended her and put some stitches in her head, but she was now all right. The Bench ordered the defendant to pay the costs— £2 10s.

div.head: STREET BETTING AT WIDNES.
div.p: STREET BETTING AT WIDNES.

At Widnes, on Thursday, Michael Collins was charged with frequenting West Bank-street for the purpose of betting.—Mr. J. W. Knowles prosecuted, and said that on the 14th inst. Detective-sergeant Davidson was concealed in the Globe Chemical Works, and he saw the defendant take slips and money from 19 men and 3 , women. When charged be replied," I didn't take money from women and children.' The defendant pleaded guilty in respect of the following day.—Superintendent Strickland said the defendant belonged to St. Helens, and had been fined there for betting.—The defendant was fined £lO and costs in each case, £33 3s. in all.—A youth named Walter Allen was also charged with using West Bank-street on the same days.—Mr. Knowles said the defendant appeared to be working for others. He was seen by Sergeant Davidson to take slips from people and give them to defendant Collins.—The bench fined the defendant 40s. and costs in each case.

THE NEW WORKHOUSE MASTER AND MATRO N. The officers of the Wolverhampton Union (exclusive of the Workhouse officers) met at the Union Offices, St, Peter's Close, Wolverhampton, on Thursday evening last week, for the purpose of offering to Mr. T. D. TtoHinson their congratulations upon his marriage, and upon the appointment of himself and his wife, to the offices of Master and Matron of the Runcorn Work- house, and of presenting to him a two-handled silver rose bowl, and to Mrs. ItoHinson a pencil case.—Mr. Prank Harrison (Clerk to the Guardians), made the presentation, speaking in eulogistic terms of the work of Mr. RoHinson during the 14 years he had been in the service of the Wolverhampton Guardians. During the time he (Mr. Harrison) had been in Wolverhampton, he had been in frequent contact with Mr. RoHinson in the discharge of his duties, and had formed the opinion that Mr. Rollinson, by his straightforwardness, ability, and earnestness of purpose, had earned the promotion to the office he was now about to occupy. In offering congratulations to Mrs. Rollison, Mr. Harrison said she had proved herself an excellent Ward Sister,doing credit to her Nottingham Training School. —Mr. RoHinson, in acknowledging, said that whilst he had been in Wolverhampton, he had made many friends, and most of those present he counted as intimate friends. The present token of good feeling was parti- cularly acceptable, and appreciated, coming as it did, from officers, so mauy of whom were not in direct association with him in his duties. He took the oppor- tunity of thanking Mr. Harrison, personally, for the kindness shown to him, and for the ever ready advice received from him, which he would strive his utmost to not upon. FRODSHAM VESTRY MEETING.

The vestry meeting was held at the Frodsham Parish Church 9n Monday morning, the vicar (Rev. H. B. Blogg), presiding over a good attendance. The vicar's warden, Mr. Thomas Riley, read the accounts for the past year. On the receipt side were included ordinary offertories, £l6O 7s. 10d.; special offertories, £l5l 18s.; early celebrations, £ll 18s. 4d.; donations for special purposes, 9s. Id. ; other sources, £27 185. 6d.; the total including the previous year's balance of £25135. 4d. being £3Bl ss. Id., or over £3O in excess of the previous year. There was a balance in hand of £l9 is. 6d., which was considered satisfactory. The number of coins offered in collections during the year amounted to 21,407 (or 1,508 in excess of the previous year),made up of thirty- three sovereigns, thirty-two half sovereigns, thirteen crowns, 185 half-crowns, 236 florins, 881 shillings, 1,960 sixpences, 2,502 threepences, 9,151 pennies, 6,111 half-pence, also bank notes and cheque to the amount of £4O 10s. The Iron Church accounts showed a balance of £2 10s. The Bridge Mission Church showed on the receipt side £3O Os. Id. and on the payment side £32 Ss. 4d., leaving a satisfactory balance of L 6 us. 91. All the accounts were passed. The various officers for the ensuing year were appointed as follows :—Vicar's warden, Mr. Thomas Riley ; parishioners' warden, Mr. J. J. Wilkinson ; sidesusen— Parish Church. Messrs. H. Tiley, E. H. Hain' vn, J. Pearson, W. G. Linaker, H. Andrew; and G. H. Midge —lron Church, Messrs. John Garner, A. Robinson, James Illidge, and John J. Nield ; Churchyard Com- mittee, Messrs. J. G. Aston, E. G. Steward, C. E. Linaker, tind J. Garner, with the vicar and two wardens • lay representatives, Messrs. W. N. Hutchings and T. DI Timmins; hon. auditor, Mr. T. D. Timmins.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
MEAN MARKET THEFT.

William Riley, of Tontine-street, was on Monday fined 7s. 6d. and costs for stealing a plant ofT a stall in the St. Helens market on Saturday night. Sr. HELENS BRUTALITY. Previous to the football match on the Sutton Com- mercial ground, St. Helens Junction, on Good Friday, a number of spectators, some of whom were wearing clogs, indulged in some indiscriminate kicking, with the result that a young man named Rimmer had his ankle injured. John Glannan, aged thirty-two, of 6, Powell-street, Sutton, had his leg fractured.

div.head: ST. HELENS WOUNDING CHARGE.
div.p: ST. HELENS WOUNDING CHARGE.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Thursday, Archibald Brown, a contractor, of 26, Dorothy-street, was again remanded for a week on a charge of unlawfully wound- ing Hobert Harris by breaking his jaw.—Mr. E. W. Swift, who appeared for the prosecution, said the injured man was still in hospital, and a further remand was necessary.—On the application of Nil% Pennington Riley, who defended, bail was allowed.

BANK HOLIDAY. St. Helens people gave themselves up to holiday- making on Monday. A large number left the town by excursion. The members of the St. Helens Camera Club paid a visit to Windermere and district. The Cyclist Club visited Chester and North Wales, where they were joined by several members of the Motor Club. The two local football matches were well patronised, and the gala which is being run this week at the Volunteer headquarters provided amusement for large numbers of people. In the evening the Theatre and Hippodrome were thronged, and the day passed off very pleasantly.

- - SAD BURNING FATALITY AT ST. HELENS. Mr. Brighouse held the inquiry on Wednesday at St. Helens Town Hall into the death of Eliza Critchley, aged three, of Clyde-street, who died in the Providence Hospital the previous day from burns.—The mother on Monday morning left deceased and a girl aged five in the kitchen. The fender was down, but there was no fireguard. In a minute or two she heard a scream, and rushed in, to find Eliza in flames. She had ouly her night clothes on, all of which were of flannelette.—The Coroner said that when the Bill that was before Parlia- ment was passed parents like this would have to pay fines for leaving children in rooms with unprotected fires. It was no good him saying anything further, but he hoped the Bill would soon become law.—The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death."
ST. HELENS GAMBLER FINED. CAUGHT WHILE WATCHING A BAND.

John Woodcock, alias Milne, of Brook-street, was charged in custody at St. Helens, on Tuesday, on four charges of betting in the streets. Detective-inspector Dunn and Police-constable Anders stated they watched the young man from a place of concealment on the nch and three following days. . They stated that they saw him receive bets from men women, and youths. He crossed backwards and forwards between the side streets from Brook-street and Water-street, and when he went into the side passages men who were watching for him directed the people to where he was located. As soon as he received the bets he went to a certain house, where it was suggested that he deposited the slips. On Monday, Anders watched him, and while his attention was drawn to a brass band that was passing the officer slipped , round the crowd and arrested him. Defendant denied the truth of the police evidence. ! He maintained that on Monday he was not out of the house five minutes before he was arrested. Anders, recalled, said that he found five betting slips in defendant's possession when he was locked up. The slips all related to Monday's betting, and represented deposits of El 2s. 21d. Alexander Milne, defendant's father, said he was with him when arrested. He denied that defendant took any beta, and said that during the time the police had said he was taking bets defendant was at dinner. In cross-examination by the Chief Constable Milne

div.head: EARLES TOWN PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: EARLES TOWN PARISH CHURCH.

The annual sermons on behalf of the Sunday schools will be preached on Sunday by the Rev.W. B.Pollock. A children's service will be held in the afternoon at three o'clock, when special hymns and recitations will be given by the choir and children.

div.head: SERIOUS SLIP ON BANANA PEEL.
div.p: A SERIOUS SLIP ON BANANA PEEL.

Whilst on duty on Saturday morning, P.C. Robert Simpson slipped on a banana peel and so severely injured himself inwardly that he had to be taken to the Royal infirmary, Liverpool, where he was operated upon on the same day. He is reported to be progressing favour- ably.

div.head: SHOP ASSISTANTS' M.P.
div.p: SHOP ASSISTANTS' M.P.

MR. J. A. SEDDON AS THE UNION CANDIDATE. The annual Conference of the National Union of Shop Assistants, Warehousemen, and Clerks was resumed at Cardiff on Monday,Mr. J. T. Duncan (Leeds) presiding.. The President moved that they appoint Mr. J. A. Seddon as their Parliamentary candidate. If the resolu- tion was carried the cost of the next election in the Newton division would, he said,devolve upon the Union and would not be less than £soo,but the cost of nursing and developing the constituency from the last to the next election would be borne by the local Labour party. The President added that the local Labour party in the Newton division had 15,000 mem- bers—more than the number of votes Mr. r_•eddon got when returned for the division. The annual cost of organising and propagating the principles that returned Mr. Seddon was OW. The President did not personally coincide with the principle adopted by the Labour party generally in the matter of nominating, running, and financing candidates, but he thought they were justified in entering into the general Labour movement and in having a representative in the House of Commons. Mr. A. Parr (Cardiff) seconded. Mr. Krayling (Waltharnstow) opposed the motion, contending that they themselves should have the oppor- tunity of selecting the candidate. At the same time he recognised that Mr. Seddon, though a miners candi- date, had done them excellent service in Parliament. Members of their own organisation might be candidates at the next election, and he would prefer to divide the money amongst them.. . .

Mr. Currie (London) also opposed, pointing out that there was a deficiency of £BOO on the management fund, and that they could not afford the proposed expenditure. The motion was carried by 112 to 21.

div.p: INDEPENDENT URDER OF RECHABITES.
Warrington District No. 4.

At the invitation of Bro.J. Hill, District Chief Ruler, the executive members of the above district, along with their wives sat down to a knife and fork tea at the Academy-street Cafe, %Warrington, on Saturday. After tea the programme took the form of a social evening, Bro. 'l'. Wiristanley D.S., acting as chairman, and on behalf of all present expressing thanks for Bro. J. Hill's kindness, in inviting the district officers and wives to tea. _ . _

-- Bro. J. HILL replied and said that it had given him very great pleasure to meet the executive officers and their wives at tca. This was only the outcome of the appreciation of the sympathy and help he had received from them during his term of offiee, and he hoped that the unity and concord that had existed amongst the district officers would remain unbroken and that all would continue to strive for the success of the Order.
bongs were given by Bro. R. Mrs. liarrison, recitations by Bro. James Shaw and B. Warburton, and several games were heartily indulged in. _

At the close of the meeting Bro. E. Walkden, District Trustee, on behalf of the members of the Executive, made a presentation to Bro. James Shaw, Senior Trustee of the District, of an English silvek lever watch as a token of their appreciation of his worg as Senior Trustee and father ot the District, havinh held that position 21 years. Bro. Walkden said that eti had known Bro. James Shaw now for a number of year and he had always been impressed with that nobleness of character and fairness of mind that set him up as an efficient officer of the District. Bros. J. Hill, J. E. Gee, T. Massey, R. Harrison, and W. \Vright expressed their admiration of the duties performed by Bro. Shaw on behalf of the District. Bro. J. SitAw in receiving the present said that. that was altogether a surprise to him, and he must say that the secret of the presentation had been well kept, as he had not beard one single word about it trail that moment. He very much appreciated the present that had been made to him, and also the many kind remarks that, had been uttered. He might say that any work he had done on behalf of the district in the past, he had fulfilled willingly, and without any expectation of reward for any services he might render. He was I pleased to accept it because it was the first present he had ever received in his life from any organisation, and he was sure it reflected the kind wishes and sympathy of the Executive.
The watch which was supplied by by Mr. S. Fernley, Bridge-street, was suitably inscribej.
FREE CHURCH COMMUNICANTS.

In view of the controversy on the decline of religious activities it is interesting to study the actual figures with regard to Church membership given in the" Free Church Year Book" which the National Free Church Council has just published. " There is a decrease of nearly 18,000 in the irimber of communicants (Free Church) " we are told. "In fact the figures show a. general tendency towards depression which appears to be due to reaction after the revival in Wales." We are told that the Free Churches now have 2,184,102 com- municants to the 2,053,445 of the Established Church. Free Church communicants of the whole world number over twenty-one millions, as against 3,730,582 of the world-wide Anglican communities. •

div.head: FISH HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE.
div.p: FISH HARVEST THANKSGIVING SERVICE.

A distinct novelty for Hull is being arranged in the fishing part of the city. A service is to be held in St. Barnabas' Church, in the Fishopolis of Hull, it being considered that the fishing industry should hold a thanksgiving for the fish that has been caught, rather than for the fruits of the earth, with which they have ,I not such close connection.

In a certain tittle rscottien tiawn, some time ago, they held a temperance meeting. During the proceedings an old man, who was not exactly celebrated, for sobriety, got up to address the audience. He said, after a few remarks upon the beautv and advantages of moderation: "My friends, there's just twa occasions when I tak' vrhi-;ky--" Undismayed by the "hums!" and which ensued, hek continued: "Ay, I just tak' whisky when I hae haggis for (leaner, and I tak whisky when I hae nae haggis—" The rest of the speech was lost in the storm of applause that broke forth. A German governess;domiciled with a Sussex family, sought, by reading and diligent observa- tion, to perfect her knowledge of our tongue: Her praetice was to refer any puzzling words to the head of the family for explanation. One morning, at bre4fast, she asked what kind of animal it was -that was' called in English "rapids." "Oh, the rabbit, Fraulein," replied Mr. C—. the rabbit is---"z "Ach,l no!" protested Franlein. "I do know the rab- bit, but this is spelt r-a-p-i-d-s, and I did' know at once it was an animal because I saw it put on a piece of music---` Shooting the Rapids." The father of a young man who had been lately 1-tarried had occasion to send a faithful but somewhat blunt old servant to his son's house, some miles distant, on business. On his return, anxious to hear the old man's opinion of the lady, said: "Well, you saw the bride, Thomas?" "Yes.. master, I saw the bride." "She's a wealthy lady, Thomas." "Yes, master, very wealthy, I suppose." "Well, and what's your el)inion, Thomae?" "J think she's a right ,nnie lady to talk to, as ,think as being rich and clever ; but, master," said the old man confiden- tially, "if beauty's a sin, she won't have that to answer for."

div.head: COMING RACE STRUGGLE.
div.p: THE COMING RACE STRUGGLE.
[By Henry Whithaml

Are coming events casting their ominous shadows before us and is the race struggle, that is certainly now on, likely to become so intensified that the dogs of war may be again loosed, and we may have once more the horrors of war upon us ? I must confess that my feelings in this matter are very pessimistic. I fear the world has now entered upon such a condition of things as it never befcre witnessed. When the late Government, at the close of the South African war, decided to furnish Asiatic labour to the Rand employer, I knew it was a great and a horrible mistake. I said so at the time, and in the "Examiner." 1 not only did this, but I furnished several lecturers with printed matter that fully des- cribed the dark ways of the Asiatic wherever he may go. It was all in vain; the Mo igolian was taken to Afrida, and I may now say, surely the reading of the history of the movement cannot be satisfactory to the British electors. Allow me again to be reminiscent. A long number of years ago, and when a Conserva- tive Government was in power, a movement was started in India intended to give the native Indian some show in the magistracy, and with the greater and much more important fea ire of educating the native Indian in the ways and methods of self- government. This was strongly resisted by the home Government. At that time a very dear friend of mine, Mr. Mall, was in the editorial department of the Warrington " Guardian." As editor and owner of an Indian paper he had had a large experience of Indian affairs, and as a meeting in support of the Government's policy was to be held. in the Public Hall the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, who then repre- sented Warrington called at the " Guardian " office seeking information on Indian affairs. The same evening, at my home, Mr. Mull told me what had passed between himself and Sir Gilbert. He had told the member for Warrington that he should be at the public meeting, and should seek permission to speak against the resolution to be put to the meeting. Of course, we expected a row, and iherefore I determined to be at the meeting and in the gallery I was perched and close to the platform. Dr. Mackie took the chair, I think, and after the opening speech called upon Sir Gilbert for a little of his brilliant oratory. This over Mr. Mull arose and asked per- mission to speak. This called for a consultation between the two pillars of society, the Dr. and the Brewer, with a refusal as the result. Mr. Mull Nish a hand-full of papers insisted upon his right to a ..ik. I also stood up and started in with a talk,and then com- menced as geed an exhibition as it is possible to have of the liberty loving Christian Tory when he is on the war path. The meeting carried its resolution in support of the Government's policy, such policy being the preventing of the native Indian from learning by experience the art of self-government. Now I want to say riEht here, the Tory Government of that day took the capital " I " out of Imperialism and ought for ever after to have spelled the word with a plain common i,' which being interpreted means slavery. Times have changed very much indeed since the happening of the episode as above narrated, but this feature is to be noted.,There were at that now distant _ day native Indians who felt they could fill the magis- trate's chair with satisfaction, at least to their own people, and there were suite a few of the governing race who felt the same, and felt also that they could be quite as impartial as the white race. I would ask, do any of those workingmen who, as government-makers, think for a moment of the wonderful advance that has been made during the past twenty-five years in the education of the best of the youth of the Asiatic races? You have in India to-day crowds of able natives who have received the highest education Europe can give. They can also make good use of it. Three days ago three shoo were fired that will most certainly resound through the length and breadth of Asia. To-day Mr. Durham White Stevens, American diplomat, lies dead as the result of those shots. I shall describe this terrible tragedy further on. For my purpose just now I wish to describe Asia as consisting of India, "the brightest gem of the British Crown," Japan having treaty rights with Great Britain, end China a place for the greedy eye of the nations to hunger after. India, what is the East Indian doing to-day ? I will try to tell you. Her myriads are seeking to better their conditions. Every day I see crowds of the poorest of these Hindoos lounging around seeking work. They have been tried on street work and on farm work. They have no women with them. The rails roadthave paid them I.Bodols. a day, but they prove to be inferior to the Japs, and so are underbidding the little brown men. It is thought that we have at least 3,000 of these Hindoo subjects of His Majesty. They will have to go. The central idea of immigration to America is the plain and simple fact that the people coming here must be of those with whotr we can assimilate. Senator Lodge speaking in Boston s3id " it may 13 frankly stated that the white race will not permit Asiatics to compete with their own labour in their own countries." Aside from this, and it has just recently been accentuated, it is best that the Asiatic and European stock should be kept apart. The United States has no entangling alliances with Asia that will give the Asiatic ccolie any rights here. It is very different with Great Britain. When Bombay, at present the second largest city in the British Empire, had br en acquired, the Government o' England, in granting it to the British East India Co., wrote the following words under the date of March 27tb, 1660: "And it is declared that all persons being His Majesty's subjects inhabiting within the said island and their children and their posterity born within the limits thereof shall be deemed free denizens and natural subjeats as if living and born in England." Queen Victoria in her letter to Lord Derby, Governor-General of India, commanding him to write the proclamation, said: " And point out the privileges which the Indians will receive in *being placed on an equality with the subjects of the British Crown, and Prosperity flowing in the train of civilization." These are very nice words and the Hindoos have read them and say in answer that" The British autocrats in India have consistently ignored them." They also assert " that after 150 years of British rule in India the people of that county are not permitted te carry arms ; that no native is appointed to any responsible position in the Army, and that he .13 excluded from the Navy, nor can he have any voice in the fiscal administration of India." Now, remember, I urn writing this with a full remembrance of 1857. "In 1870 competitive examinations for the Indian Civil Service were opened to Indians as well as to Europeans." This is a true stateinent ; it also bides the truth. These examina- tions are held only in England, and under conditions which practically shut out the _lndians from civil service. Repeatedly have the Indian leaders requested the British Government to hold these civil sex vice examinations simultaneously in' ladia, but an emphatic negative answer is always returned. Mr. Gokhale a member of the Indian Viceroy's Council, and a level-headed Indian politic:an says "Our net revenue is about £4.1,C30,000 sterling. Of this vet/ nearly one-half is eaten up by the army. The home charges, exclusive of the military portion, absorb nearly on( th;rd. rhen more than £3,000,000 is paid to European officials in civil service. This leaves about £7.000,000 at the disposal of the Government for other purposes." But now comes the deadly comparison and this native Indian knows how to make it: ".,Can anyone wonder that the Govern- ment spends only a miserable threequarters of a million out of the State funds on the education of the 1720p1e ? Japan came under the influence of Western ideas only forty years ago, and yet already she is in line with the most advanced nations of the West in matters of education, the State finding funds for the leducation of eveiy child of school-going age. We I have now been a hundred years under England's rule and yet to-day four villages out of every five are with- out a school-house, and seven children out of every eight are allowed to grow up in ignorance and dark- ness. Militarism, service interests, and the English capitalists' interests all take precedence to-day, of the true interests of the Indian people in the administra- tion of the countti."

Is it neces..ary to say more in condemnation of the policy hitherto pursued in Inda? Truly it is time that caste government was abolished and the proletariat given a chance. ,This is the position and it should be understood if you don't want. the Empire to go overboard before tbe next twenty-five years go by. The Japanese heat the migllty Russian Empire and all Asia knows it. The Hindoo, the Jap, the Korean and the Chinese have all been onside of Asia, and.they know all about the Western conditions. By treaty rights the most important of the nations I have mentioned have a legal right to come and settle in Warrington and to enter into competition with the iron workers and the tradesmen, and you cannot

possibly hinder them when once their faces are turned towards Europe. Your treaty with Japan was a bad Move, and the brown man will only hold to it so long as it snits his purpose. You have seen the depths of his cunning in Manchuria and in Seoul, Korea. It is utterly impossible for the stay-at-home English- man to understand the Orientals. I may go farther and say -that it is impossible for the globe-trotting Britisher to know them. The former never comes in contact with them at all, and the latter merely sees them when they have their company manners on duty. Twenty , years ago we in San Francisco knew little or nothing of , the Jap. One or two shops in the main street covered their business, now we have thousands. On the street, the ferry, the train, the car and in the store, the Japs are everywhere, In the country they are masters of the situation. Wherever they settle they Flictate terms. They can do this because cf labour being scarce. The economic and climatic conditions make farm labour impossible to the white man, so the Jap and the Chinaman compete, the latter coming out second best, and, as a rule he seems anxious to give the Jap all the room he wants. When the Jap has fixed himself in a country district he waits patiently until he sees his chance and then a wage question is on. He gets what he wants and than he wait i a little longer until he finds a farm for sale or rent. He then makes a bid and unless he gets it on terms to snit himself he just boycotts it, and there is no race of men on earth who understand how to make a labour organization effective like the Oriental. So far as the United States goes what I have said touching immigration applies to East and West alike, with certain well understood qsalifications. San Francisco seems doomed to have more than its share of the world's trouble. Now it is a shooting trouble, and as it happens to be one of the governing caste who, for a consideration condescends to govern us, who has been shot to death, it follows that the various chancellories concerned will show some activity. The story in brief is that a couple of young Korean boys determined to avenge their country for some insulting language, as the Koreans thought it, given out to the Press by Mr. Stevens. These Koreans have a Mission school at which they hold meetings nightly. They also have a minister, the Rev. C. S. Ryang, a Korean, and while he prayed the Koreans discussed the speech of Mr. Stevens as reported in the Press. The following day Mr. Stevens, leaving for an Eastern State, was met at the ferry by the two Koreans, one of whom did all the shooting. He shot his own accomplice, and as it has since proved, shot Mr. Stevens to the death. The following is a statement made by In Wham Chang in explanation and justification of his act. Translated, the statement read? : My country is completely wrecked by the Japanese since the Japanese protection. Mr. Stevens helps to make out the plan to destroy Corea, for he was appointed adviser in the interest of Japan, and as he said here, he is a great friend of Japan. He did many things cruel to Coreans through Japanese for Japan's sake while he was paid by the Corea.n Government to do service for Corea. While he was in Corea he appeared to do something for Corea but that was all chceting in reality. He said I was a fool and misunderstood the situation, but that is a part of his plan to cheat other people. He has come to the United States to tell the _people the same false tales that he told here, and if I had cared for my life and let him go on to do it, the hope of my country would have been gone for ever. On account of the restrictions placed on her by the other countries of the world Japan is not able to do all the things in Corea that they would like. Therefore, Japan made out a plan to send Stevens into the United States under the title of "American Adviser to Cores" to make the people to believe, or to cheat them to believe that the Japanese con- trol is' beautiful in Corea. He said in the papers that ha is a great friend to Corea, but that is what he says, and he says it to make the people to believe what else he says. Why would I not kill him ? Thousands of thou- sands of people have been through his plan, and as much will be killed if he returns to Corea from United Status America. So I shot him for the sake of my country and to sympathize with the people who have already been killed, and to save the r uople from another killing by Stevens. What is life? Everybody ought to know how to die. If I kill him and die it will be glory to my country and happy to the people. WHAN CHANG. I have given the above in full because I want my readers to fully understand the mind of the Asiatic. You may spend your money on missions and you may think you have civilized him but if ever you make the slightest scratch you will certainly find the Asiatic. A suggestive feature of the shooting of Mr. Stevens is that it should have been done by Koreans. We of the Pacific Coast scarcely knew of them and certainly gave them little notice. We took them to be a quiet, simple, and inoffensive people, and suddenly the world hears of two Korean boys, armed with a revolver, that is little more than a boy's cheap toy pistol with a barrel an inch and a half long, shooting an American statesman. If a Korean can in so cool a fashion take his life in his hands, what may we expect of the more warlike Asiatic ?

We may rest assured that the conflict between thel Western and the Asiatic races is not merely impend- ing, it is on. It is a mighty struggle for the mastery of the Pacific. The white races of Europe have tried many times for the mastery in Asia, but have never succeeded in gaining it, or of keeping it for long, and in doing so they have taught the dark races 'he use of the weapons used by Europeans. Japan has learned not only the use of the weapon, but the industrial methods of the white nations. She is teaching China, she is influencing India. In 1857 the East Indian knew little outside of his own country. This is all altered. The editor of on Indian paper, the "Sand Rya" who is now serving two years in prison for seditious writing, wrote :—" We know for certain that you will not live long here ; the Moguls, the Pathans, the Hindus, the Portuguese, the French, all have come and gorse, and so will you too." ' Now, what is the moral of all this? Those who are interested will find it well given in the " Pnblic Opinion," Felarusay 7, page 1 and paragraph 3. There is a deal more to he said on this question, Canada and An tralia are,as important features in.the British Empire, interested in the Asiatic emigrant, Alameda, California.
WHI'ItAM.
The Examiner, Saturday April 25, 1908.

It will be seen that, although we have no cotton duties and although America is the producer of the material, America is practically unable to sell cotton goods here. But the figures given, interesting and instructive as they are, do not do justice to the extra- ordinary facts of the case, which ought to be known to every elector of the United Kingdom. The cotton trade is one of cur staples. Whether we ourselves are engaged in it, or whether wa live hundreds of miles from Lancashire, it means much to us. Whether we work in Dundee or the Midlands, in Yorkshire or London, in Wales or the Eastern Counties, we gain by the great cotton trade. It sets up a stream of wealth which flows through every town and village in the country. To lose the cotton trade would be irrepar- able. What Tariff Reformers are doing by misrepre- sentation is to persuade the British people to strike a deadly bloz at Lancashire and therefore at themselves. If they told their audiences the truth about the cotton trade alone the Tariff Reform agitation would collapse.
itritich and American eatton Hai/arts
Let us contrast British and American exports of cotton manufacauss in 1906 and 1907 :--
BRITISH AND AMERICAN EXPORTS OF COTTON MANUFACTURES. 1906. 1907. ' £ Exports from the United Kingdom 99,600,000 110,400,000 Exports from United States

Such are the figures which are so carefully concealbd by Tariff Reform orators. In 1907 we exported twenty-two times more cotton goods than the United States of Ameiica. Yet we had first to buy our raw cotton from America, being forbidden by nature to grow it ourselves. It may be added that there is no other country which in the cotton or any other trade exports £100,000,000 of goods in one branCh alone. It is an industrial miracle, this cotton trade of ours. British and American Cotton Imports
_ But even more remarkable are the facts as to imports. Let us set out in the same way:—
BRITISH AND AMERICAN IMPORTS OP COTTON MANUFACTCRES. 1908. 1907. Imports into United Kingdom 9,300,000 9,500,CC0 Imports into TT ....(1 t 13,800,000 15,900,C DO United.-433

Few Tariff Reformers know of these facts and, it may be added, that if these facts were universally known, there would be few Tariff Reformers. Hero we : -e the United Kingdom, with ports open to all the world, importing only £9,500,000 worth of cotton goods in 1907 while America with the Dingley Tariff doing its best to shut out cotton goods, importing £15,90,000 worth in the same period. Let us remind ourselves of the American cotton duties. I give a few specimens.

SOME AMERICAN IMPORT DUTIES ON COTTON MANUFACTURES. Coloured cotton yarn, all counts up to No. 20, 3 pen' 3 per lb. Cottnn cloth, unbleached, not exceeding 50 threads per square inch, Id, per square yard. Ditto exceedigg 300 threads, 2 pence per square yard. Cotton Stockings, 30 per cent ad valorem.
Cotton Table Damask 40 per cent ad valoeem.

It is in spite of duties like these that America imports about £16,000,000 of cotton goods in a year against our £9,500,000. That is how Protection fails to protect. Handicapped by her tariff policy, America cannot compete with us in a trade in which she ought easily to beat us.

Here is one-sided Free Trade with a vengeanco. America unable to sell hero in a free importing country; Britain largely selling in America in spite of the ditties. I repeat that it is not Lancashire alone sOich is concerned in the facts I have related. The interests of Lancashire are the common interests of the nation. We cannot afford to disturb our cotton trade and nothing is more certain than that its eristence would be reduced to a struggle under Protection. The cotton trade needs Free IMports if it is to prosper, not Free Trnports of raw cotton alone, but free imports of every food stuff, raw material, and manufactured material. Cotton goods aze not made of cotton alone but of steel and brick, and cement, and glass, and oil and leather, and dye and filling and every other com: modity which is used in connection with the buildings or machinery in which they tiN fabricated. The cotton trade is a standing proof of the wisdom Of fighting foreign tariffs with Free Imports, and it is in grave peril as long as the Protectionist agitation continues.

MY DEAR CHILDREN, I hope all of you will spend a very happy Easter. .1 am writing my weekly chat just before the holidays. I expect you have all 'a short holiday from school. I hope you will have fine fun. I don't really believe that many of you know when the four seasons of the year commence; at least, the answers received do not, by any means, agree! After carefully going through all the replies, I have decided to send a prize to Happy Copp. I also send one to Florence Dark. This member com- menced her definition very well, but evidently the season of Spring upset it somewhat! Now, as to the reason of Easter being a Mov- able Feast. Many of my members were evi- dently puzzled by Easter, and, consequently, sent in very vague answers. I have pleasure in awarding the prize to Ida Bow. Gwendoline Kivell carries off the prize for "Spending Easter Monday." Oh, I forgot, there is the award for the best picture of myself. Now, to be quite honest, none of the sketches were like me. I think that the one sent in by Cecil Fishef is the best, only I should have been drawn wearing spectacles. Well, Cecil, I think I will send you the prize, as you have all had to work in the dark on this subject. . This Sketching Competition has been very successful, so I propose to have another one. Next week I will give full particulars. •With love, UNCLE 4 NED.

div.head: GOING ON AN ERRAND.
div.p: GOING ON AN ERRAND.

A pound of tea, at one and three, A pot of raspberry jam, Two new-laid eggs, a dozen pegs, And a pound of rashers of ham. I'll say it over all the way, s And then I'm sure not to forget; " For if chance to bring things wrong, My mother has cause to fret. A pound of tea, at one and three, •A pot of raspberry jam, Two new-laid eggs, a dozen pegs, And a pound of rashers of ham. There in the hay the children play; They're having such lots of fun; I'll go there, too—that's what I'll do— As soon as my errands are done. A pound of tea, at one-and-three, A pot of er—er—new-laid jam, Two raspberry eggs, a dozen pegs, And a pound of rastiers of ham. There's Teddy White, flying. his kite, He thinks himself grand, I declare; I'd like to try, I'd go sky-high, Yes, ever so much higher, • Above the old church spire, And then—but there— A pound of three, at one—and tea, A pot of new-laid jam, Two dozen eggs, some raspberry pegs, And a rash of pounders of ham. Now, here's the shop, outside I'll stop, And say my orders again; I haven't forgot, no, ne'er a jot, My memory's good, that's plain. A pound of three, at one—and tea, A dozen of raspberry ham. A pot of eggs, with a pound of pegs, And a rasher of new-laid jam. \ H. Corp.

div.head: LION AND THE MOUSE.
div.p: THE LION AND THE MOUSE.

A lion once had fallen asleep, when a little mouse began to climb over his back. This awoke the lion, and he put out his big paw and caught the mouse. But the mouse pleaded so hard that the lion (et him go. About twelve months after, the lion Was caught himself in a net prepared by some hunters. He roared in anger, and tried to get out, but could net, when the little mouse happened to pass by and heard the lion's voice, and recognised it, and straightforth went and began to gnaw the net- work, and finally set the lion free. RUBY LAW SC N.

div.head: BROOM AND THE BEARD.
div.p: THE BROOM AND THE BEARD.

A man once went into a barber's shop in Glasgow to get shaved. He was a Highlander, from the West 'of Scotland, and he made his living by selling brooms. The barber bought one, and, after he had finished shaving him, asked what was the price of it "Twopence." But the barber thought that was too much. "Here is a penny," he said, "and if you are not oontented with that, you can take back the broom." The Highlander took back the broom, and, then asked what he had to pay for being shaved. "A penny." The High- lander pulled out a halfpenny and gave it, to the barber. "If you are not contented with that," he said, "you may put on my beard again." LIZZIE KIRBY.

f SHADOWS. ' I like to play shadows with Teddy .When the nursery lamp is lit, And across the floor and on the wall Our funny black pictures flit. Sometimes they're tiny, like goblins grim; Then we move, and they quickly grow; I wish we grew as fast, but, perhaps, Only shadows the secret know. They never make the slightest sound, No matter how noisy, our play; When we dance and run, they follow its In the queerest, quietest way. And once Teddy drew my shadow, And we blacked it over with ink; Ted says its exactly like me, But it's rather too ugly. I think. JAMES HENRY DONE.

Caterpillars are mostly covered with short halts or bristles. They may crawl over one's skin without the slightest inconvenience, but immediately on being handled these bristles break off and stick in the skin, and the more one tries to brush them off the more they spread. The greatest offender is the larva of the "brown-tailed' moth" found in the early part of June on the hawthorn.

Nobody has yet been able to solve satisfactorily the mystery of the swifts' migration. The birds do not arrive in these islands until May, and yet they are for the most part ready to go by the middle of August. The first north-west wind after that date generally decides the question for the majority, but there are always a few laggards, who remain until the end of the month. A swift is a rare sight in September.

div.head: KING AND A ZAM-BIIK HERO.
div.p: THE KING AND A ZAM-BIIK HERO.
MINE EXPLOSION SEQUEL.
Terrible Sores and Inflammation Healed.

The heroism of pit workers has of late been well before the public. Renee the gratitude of Mr: Francis Chandler, of 103, Church Street, plump, near Barnsley, when Zam-Buk healed his terrible injuries in time to permit him to go before His Majesty the King and receive the first Miner's V.C. for his heroism in the floyland Silkstone Explosion is both topical and instructive. Complications from blood-poisoning were apparently only prevented by the timely use of this famous balm. " When I came out of hospital my hands arid arms were very s ,re and tender,' said Mr. Chandler in an interview with the " Barnsley Chronicle" reporter.. "There was pain all along the scalded parts ; some- times it was a dull, throbbing pain, at other times the rain would shoot sharply from wrist to finger tips, making me catch my breath in agony. Almost all the skin had been taken from the backs of my hands by ppthe scalding steam, and the thin layer of skin that had grown over while I was in the hospital was so flimsy and tender that the slightest knock or rub would bring a piece off. My right wrist was particularly troublesome. There were also one or two nasty look- ing sores on my hands that seemed /ilsdy,to turn to blood poison. " Just about Xmas a friend of mine, who noticed how the pain was' ' me, persuaded me to try some Zam-Buk, and she gave me a little out of her box ; rand this did me so much good that I got a box fortmyself. I applied the rich balm on the sore parts night and morning. The flesh was so very raw,tender and sore, that it was only after I had persevered with Zam-Buk that the pain was lessened. I now dressed the injured parts more freely with Zam-Buk, the balm causing a new and stronger skin to grow over the sore places ; and my hands were consequently not nearly so tender. The muscles of the wrist which had grown very stiff, became quite flexible. I kept on tubbing Zam-Buk in until at last all the pain and soreness had completely gone. Now I can use my hands and twist them about almost as well as ever, and they are covered with a strong, healthy skin. "The nasty looking sores that seemed likely to turn to blood poison are quite healed up, and are now as healthy looking as the rest of my hands. Zam-Buk has done wonders for me.'.' While from time to time much remarkable proof of the uniqueness and excellence of Zam-Buk has been published, the testimony of Mr. Chandler is testimony of unusual distinction. Zam-Buk is composed of certain rare herbal saps and juices that distinguish it from all old-fashicnedi ointments and salves.

div.p: Warrington's Visit to London.

In order to further popularize Northern Union foot- ball in the metropolis, a match was arranged on Satur- day between Wakefield Trinity and Warrington at the Memorial Grounds, West Ham, a silver cup being pre- sented for competition. There was only a small attend- ance; less than 1,000 spectators being present. Warring- ton had rather a weak side, but the Trinitarians were strongly represented, and succeeded in winning the match. The teams were : Warrington : Jordan, back ; Fish, Dickenson, Cart- I wright, and Foster, three-quarter backs ; Brooks and ; Lloyd, half backs; A. Boardman, Jolley, P. Birdman, Harmer, Heath and Naylor, forwards. Wakefield Trinity : Metcalfe, back; Simpson, McPhail, Sidwell, and Bennett, threequarter backs ; Ward and Slater, half backs ; Crossland, Walton, Taylor, Unsworth, Beaumont, and Auton, forwards. Referee, Mr. Priest- ; ley, Salford. Warrington got away in the first minute, and scored a try through Cartwright, Fish 'failing at the goal-kick. , Sidwell missed a penalty kick, and just afterwards ; Slater initiated a fine bout of passing, Simpson getting , over, but Metcalfe failed to convert. From a scrum- , mage the ball came out to McPhail, who raced away , and passed- to Simpson, and the latter again scored. This try was also unconverted, and at half-time Wake- I field Trinity led by six points to three. Warrington ! soon equalized after the interval, Jordan scoring a nice try near the corner. Dickenson failed at goal. A free ' kick to Wakefield resulted in a goal being kicked by ; Slater. Continuing to have the best of matters, Wake- ; field quickly obtained another try, Simpson once more crossing the line. Metcalfe failed at goal. The play was fast and exciting, Fish putting in some splendid ; efforts without success. Result ;—Wakelleld Trinity, I one goal and three tries (eleven points) ; Warrington two tries (six points).

THE WELSHMEN.

This match was played on Monday at Tonypandy, before about 12,000 spectators in fair weather. Dai Jones started the ball against The wind, and Wales were at once pressed. Burgham gained ground subsequently, but from a penalty Jolley dropped a goal. Fish nearly got in with a smart run, and Spencer almost got over from a bout of passing, being tackled on the boundary. England again assumed the aggressive, and Birch handling from a scrummage, scored, but Jolley's kick for goal went wide. From the following play Treherne received a wide pass from J. Thomas, and scored a fine try, which D. Thomas converted. England then invaded and Spencer receiving from Hogg got in nicely, Fish converting. Spencer was injured and retired. Treherne then made a sensational run three-quarters the length of the field and scored, J. Thomas converting. Ruddick added a try, which Thomas also majorised.l Fish ran through the defence in the Welsh '25," scoring and converting. Spencer now resumed. Fish, with a fine run again scored an unconverted try, and at half-time England were leading by 3 goals, 4 tries (18 points), to Wales 3 goals, 3 tries (15 points). Wales opened the second half in determined style, and play had not \been in progress five minutes before Phil Thomas made a tine run in the centre, and ran up to Taylor before passing to Burgham, who scored. Thomas converted. Play was in favour of Wales, and good work by Dai Thomas saw Johnny Thomas cross, but he was re-called. After Hogg had been stopped by Chick Jenkins the Welsh backs brought off a fine movement, which ended in Dai Thomas running behind the posts. Johnny Thomas again converted. England, who had scarcely been over the half-why, showed chpital combination among the backs, and Batten, who was last to receive punted on, but Chick Jenkins saved cleverly. Bert Jenkins scored twice just before the finish, .1. Thomas again converting on each occasion. The match ended—Wales, 7 goals and 7 tries (35 points) ; England, 3 goals and 4 tries (18 points). Buckler (Salford), G. Rnddick (Broughton Rangers), Dai Jones and D. B. Davies (Merthyr), Oliver Burghare and J. Saunders (Ebbw Vale), forwards. Referee, Mr. R. Robinson, Bradford.

The floral decorations, which were particulaily beautiful,were carried out by Mrs.Buckton, Miss Jackson, Mrs. Young and the Misses Hirtles. Both morning and evening services went most heartily, the choir acquitting themselves creditably. The canticles were Jackson's service In F. The morning anthem was was Turner's "Christ is risen," the base solo being excellently sung by Mr. Samuel Oddy. In the evening Simper's" Christ our Passover "was nicely rendered, the treble solo being sweetly sung by Master Wilfred Fryer. The Rev. E. Harris, of Southport, officiated hroughout. •

I It is quite clear from this that Sir William paid for - the Coach and Horses the Market price at the time—he did not pay a penny piece more because the vendor was the War Office. I That really is the vital point to be considered. Did the purchaser of the Coach and Horses pay more than he would have done if he had bought it from a private individual ? If not, why should he be in any different position from that of any other public-house purchaser? Did the War Office guarantee the permanence of the value of the licence ? Of course not. What happened was exactly comparable to what takes place in the case of Death Duties. There the State merely takes its percentage on the market-value of the dead roan's estate, and if that includes a public-house, well, duty must be paid on what the public-house is worth. This does not mean that the State thinks the market-value the real value, or enters into a covenant never to do anything to alter the value. The purchaser of the Coach and Horses gave £lO,OOO because he thought that to be the value of what he was buying. If he paid too I much he must blame his own judgment, and not com- plain because the vendor happened to be a Government Department selling the property in ordinary course. ' Dr. Macnamara. M.P. THE FUNERAL. SERVICE TO BE HELD I WESTMINSTER ABBEY. The first part of the funeral service will be held at Westminster Abbey at noon on Monday next, and the burial will take place at Meigle on Tuesday. The news of Sir Henry's death was received at Stirl- ing with great regret by all parties. The town bells were tolled and flags flown at half-mast. The spot in Meigle churchyard, Perthshire, where Sir Henry will be buried beside his wife, is marked by a simple granite tablet on the wall with the words, inscribed in Italian and English . _ _ -
"My trnst is in the tender mercy of God for ever and ever."
THE BYE-ELECTION.

In regard to the political position in Stirling Burghs, the Unionists have had a candidate in the field for some time in Mr. William Whitelaw, who formerly sat for Perth City, and unsuccessfully contested Banffshire at the last election. The Liberals are unprepared. Sir Henry a fortnight ago placed himself unreservedly in the hands of the Executive and wished to resign, but the Executive desired him to stay on. No action will be taken until Sir Henry's funeral. COMPARED WITH GLADSTONE. Speeing at the mid-day service at the City Temple, London, on Thursday, the Rev. R. J. Campbell paid a touching tribute to the ex-Premier. He said in certain respects his influence over his party was greater even than that of Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone was a far more commanding personality, but he was never followed with greater respect and confidence than the statesman who has just passed away.

GENERAL BOTHA'S TRIBUTE. The "Daily Chronicle" publishes the following special cable from General Louis Botha,Prime Minister of the Transvaal :—" Have learned with deenest sorrow of the passing of Sir H. Campbell-Bannerman, in whom the Empire loses one of its wisest statesmen and the Transvaal one of its truest friends. In securing self- government for the new colonies he not only raised an imperishable monument to himself, but, through the policy of trust, he inspired the people of South Africa with a new feeling of hopefulness and co-operation. In making it possible for the two races to live and work together harmoniously he has laid the foundation of a united South Africa."

Little Jack Horner sits in the corner, Nursing a terrible cold, The chills and ills that his little frame fills' Would take a large book to unfold; He's sneezed and snuffled, grumbled and ached For days—but he'll no longer endure Such miserable torments, for see in his hands He has Woods' Great Peppermint Cure.—Advt.

div.head: Call to Arms
div.p: A Call to Arms

for Members of the Liberal Association. I Mr. C. E. Parker, the President of the Liberal Associa- tion, has addressed the following circular to the mem- bers :—" Gentlemen, It appears fitting in view of the immense importance attaching to the fate of the Licensing Bill now before Parliament, and the character and methods of the opposition, that the members of this Association should meet to confer as to the best means of giving support to the Government. It will he unworthy of our Association if in Warrington it surrenders the right to stand in the front rank in tum conflict. It is a concern of the first importance to the Liberal Party that this measure should become law. The Government have courageously taken their fate in both hands and will stand or fall with the Bill. They are furthering the cause of social progress by proposing to limit the powers of a great monopoly, which has grown to be a menace to the well-being of the State. The Bill, while leaving ample opportunity for those who desire reasonable faallities for obtaining intoxi- cating liqours, makes provision for reducing the many unnecessary temptations which, in the case of those of weak will, and perverted appetite, too often prove their personal undoing and throw upon the sober class of the community heavy burdens. The Bill gives to the people the power effectually to control a traffic which closely affects the life, well-being,and prosperity of the community. The opposition is stooping to intimidation, exaggeration, and falsehood ; every sordid motive, every selfish interest being appealed to. Surely a policy so begotten, and furthered, will not be allowed to triumph. To our Party locally the issue is as important as it is critical. The Trade has become so linked with the Con- servative Party that it seems to have added their political association to its tied house system ; it is difficult now for anyone to think of the two apart. While this in the long run may prove to the advantage of the political party, for the present it means that we will have to fight the natural forces of Conservatism allied with, or swallowed up by, a powerful monopoly which threatens to control and dominate the municipal life of the Borough. This monopoly makes no secret that its trade is its politics. In the words of the Executive of the National Trade Defence Fund, its object is " to secure by all legal means regardless of party politics, the return to the House of Commons and other elected bodies, of candidates favourable to Trade interests." Unhappily the interest of this trade is opposed to that of all other industries inasmuch as the excessive amount (averaging over five shillings a week for every working-class family) spent in drink absorbs the available spending power which if diverted to those trades providing the necessaries and comforts of life would give that much needed impetus to healthy industries which would produce that activity and prosperity which we all desire to see. We cannot shut our eyes to the fact that it is the declared policy of the Trade to capture and control municipalities by packing the Councils with direct ! and indirect representatives of the trade. This determined policy has lately met with success in ' our Borough, and we are openly threatened with their intention to capture the representation of every ward in town. The representation of particular interests always involves a danger to the general good, but if we admit it at all in connection with trade, this industry is at present represented out of all proportion to its importance. The policy which aims at securing the control of the Council constitutes a grave danger to the public well-being and Liberals should realize the danger and unite to avert it. How for example can the police feel confidence in doing their duty if they come under the control of a Council and Watch Committee largely composed of men, who (whatever be their personal ability and integrity, and these we do not -question) naturally, and by their own assertions place the interests of their own trade first? Our party stands for the rights of the people irrespec- tive of selfish trade interests. We stand for the people's right to control this, and every other monopoly in the public interest, to demand for the poor, the weak, for the women, for the children, those conditions and surroundings of life which will give them a fair chance of developing the best within them. No municipality can deal impartially with this powerful interest if it becomes dominated and degraded by those whose direct financial concern is to foster this trade. Liberals of Warrington rally to the support of your Party and Government, prepare yourselves for work, and if need be for sacrifice, and give the Executive your support by attending a meeting hereby convened on Tuesday, April 28th, at 7.30 p.m., in the Liberal Club for the purpose of conferring and taking action with a view of giving to the Government measure your united, strenuous and enthusiastic support. Resolutions will be proposed expressing our great sorrow at the loss of the ex-Premier and of confidence in the new Premier and the reconstructed Government. Yours very truly, CHARLES E. PARKER, President.

U just one of those shrewd, slow-moving designs charac- teristic of the Prime Minister. The sting of the resolu- tion was in its tail. The Lords were to be given many chances, but always at the end there was the power to override their veto. The Tories professed to laugh. But the resolution at once began to affect the situation. Faced with the possibility of destruction, the Lords moved more warily. They still destroyed, but they destroyed more shrewdly. Their prey was chosen from remoter fields. The Scotch bills were thrown out, but the English Smelt Holdings Bill and the Irish Evicted Tenants Bill were both passed. Meanwhile Sir Henry moved steadily ahead with his programme. One of his first steps this session was to pass a special, unprecedented guillotine resolution whereby the Scotch bills were to be sent up to the Lords in very quick time. This was really the first step in adopting the policy of the House of Lords resolution. Then came the attack of influenza, and the long, weakening illness which necessitated his resignation of the Premiership at the beginning of April. EPITOME OF HIS ILLNESS. It will be remembered that in November last, after a week of heavy engagements, Sir Henry addressed a large meeting in Bristol, and later in the same night he was suddenly taken alarmingly ill. He very speedily rallied, and was able to return to London in two days' time. At the end of November he went to Biarritz,and remained there until January 16th, when he left for Paris, returning to London on January 20th. Owing to a cold contracted on the way home, Sir Henry was obliged to remain indoors, and was not present at the opening of Parliament. On Sunday, February 2nd, he was, however, able to go to Buckingham Palace, where he had an audience of the King, and on February 3rd he spoke in the House. On February 12th he again made a speech, and in the evening was cheerful and not overtired. The next day, February 13th, he was not at all well, and speedily the symptoms of influenza became apparent. The attack was a sharp one, but for a time Sir Henry held his own. A few weeks later, during the night, he had a serious heart attack, and from that time his heart gradually failed. Dr. Burnet, in an interview, remarked that Sir Henry was a most plucky patient, who was always pleasant and never complained. Towards the close of his illness he knew he was dying, but he bore up with the greatest fortitude. It was about that time that he resigned the Premiership. The veteran statesman, Dr. Burnet added was greatly gratified by the visit of the King, and was also most pleased with the solicitude shown during his illness by his many friends.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Midnight Wedding."
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE. "The Midnight Wedding."

A romantic play with the above title has attracted large audiences to the Royal Court Theatre this week. Mr. Walter Howard is a master of melodrama and "The Midnight Wedding "is written in his best style. The plot is ingeniously worked out, exciting incidents abound, and there is not an uninteresting moment from the rise to the fall of the curtain. The story hinges on the wedding at midnight of Princess Astrea Von Strelsburg and Paul Valmar (swordmaster to the Red Hussars) which takes place in the first act. It is purely a matter of expediency, the Princess, under her father's will, having the alternatives of marrying before she reaches her twenty-first birthday or entering a Convent. Moreover the man she is expected to' marry is one Captain Von Scrasbruck for whom she has an utter loathing. In the nick of time, Paul Valmar, a total stranger, appears on the scene and obligingly agrees to go through the marriage with the Princess to relieve her from her unenviable position. 1 How the pair soon conceive a real affection for each other suffer much through the villainy of the rejected suitor, and are finally happily re-united is well told in the play which•has been most appreciatively received by large audiences nightly. Messrs. A. Paumier and W. Howard's Company is a thoroughly capable one. Mr. Frank E. Petley achieves a notable triumph as Paul Valmar, his fine soldierly: bearing and perfect self- possession, eminently fitting him for an exacting part: Miss Ethel Bracewell quite captivates the audience by her natural yet powerful acting as Princess Astrea Von Strelsburg. Mr. A. E. Winnington Barnes is a capital Captain Von Scrasbruck whose vindictiveness has such an important bearing on the plot. All the other roles were pleasingly sustained. The humorous aide of the play is particularly good and for this Messrs. Oscar Power J. E. Abbott and G. Scully as Sergeant Max, Corporal Otto and Private Bobbo (comrades in war but rivals in love) and Miss Lizzie Chambers as the pert Kathie of "The Golden Dragon " are mainly responsible,their escapades being a source of never wfailing merriment. The scenery is on an elaborate and artistic scale.

Next week the attraction will be a drama entitled "An unwedded wife," a powerful and fascinating play abounding in startling dramatic incidents relieved by gen line comedy.
