div.head: VIOLENT RUFFIAN.
div.p: A VIOLENT RUFFIAN.

Smart Sentence at Warrington. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday Edward Mullen, D ial-street, a well-known character, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Wednesday night, atni.with assaulting Police-Constable Kenwright and Superintendent Heap. He was further charged with having been convicted of assaults on the police during the last two years. Police-Constable Kenwright stated that the prisoner bad been ejected from the Lion Hotel Vaults, and he asked him to move on. Prisoner said witness would not shift him, and struck him a violent blow in the eye. When the prisoner was being placed in the cell he struck Sergeant Heap a violent blow on the nose. The Chief Constable said the prisoner had 17 previous convictions against him, including several terms of imprisonment for larceny and assaults on the police. Prisoner, after being sentenced to nine months' imprisonment, remarked, "If I had a revolver I would shoot him (Kenwright). They are the biggest lot of perjurers in the North of England."

div.p: THE EASTER HOLIDAYS.

INTERESTING GOLF MATCHES.

'The Paris edition of the "New York Herald," April 18th, contains the following notes on the golf at Cannes in which the Borough Member and his wife have been playing a prominent part. " Continued life is also shown at the Golf Club where the game is still strong. The Grand Duke 'Cyril is indefatigable, and rarely misses his two rounds a day. The Grand Duchess Victoria Feodorovna is constantly there, while such devotees of golf as Mr. J. B. Dugdale, Mr. E. H. Topham, Mr. Martin van Buren and Mr. S. Ward Doubleday are daily on the horizon. Yesterday some sixty or more were at the club, and about twenty-five were at the midday meal. Among them were Countess E. Apraxine, Sir John. Dunne, Countess Clara Schulen- burg, Miss Keyser, Sir John Brunner, Mr. Hervey, Mr. Elger and Mrs. Paul Nelki. At the Geisha Cottage, too, there was a gathering for breakfast at the invitation of Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfield. It was the first really pleasant old-time April day in two weeks, and the meal under the thatched veranda, amid the climbing roses, recalled the heyday of the cottage. Mrs. Crosfield's guests included the Grand Duke and the Grand Duchess Cyril, the Grand Duke Michael and Countess Torby, the Rajah of Pudukota, Lady Blythswood, Lord and Lady Cheylesmore, Mrs. Francis L. Ogden, Mr. and Mrs. John Magee, Major and Mrs. Clayton, Captain and Mrs. Godfrey-Fausett, Mr. J. M. Paulton, Mr. Montagu Elliott, Mr. G. M. Mc Namara, Mr. Ludwig Neumann, and Mr. Drummond. ! Afterwards the Grand Duke Michael played a round wita Mr. Elliott. The Grand Duke Cyril had a trial ' two club match with Mr. Crosfield, in view of an approaching competition, and the Grand Duchess Cyril played a like match with Mrs. Crosfield. Lord Cheylesmore engaged his two sons. Lord and Lady Wolverton automobiled out, and were soon busy playing. Lord Newborough, jusl; returned from 'Biarritz, was practising. Lord Salville and Mr. W. James were other players. A match that excited a good deal of interest and speculation was played on Tuesday by the Grand Duke Michael and Mr. Topham against Lord Chelsea and Mr. Paulton. The latter couple took the lead in the early part of the game which, to quote an enthusiastic golfer, " was quite a ' pull devil, pull baker' struggle all the way round,"but in the end the Grand Duke and Mr. Topham won by two up. The same afternoon Mr. A. Cameron, playing against Mr. Doubleday, holed out in 82, an identical performance with that of his second round, when he won the President's gold cigarette case during the Spring meeting. Recently, too, the Grand Duke and Grand Duchess Cyril won a match against the Grand Duke Michael and Countess Torby, Afterwards the Grand Duke Cyril and Mlle. Merlin lost a hard-fought game against the Grand Duchess and Calloway. [Another capital match was played by the Grand 'Duchess and Mr Crosfield against Mrs. Crosfield and ' Mr. Moseley, and it was won by the former couple by wo up.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Wycliffe Church. The Sunday school anniversary services will be held to-morrow (Sunday) when the preacher will be the Rev. Prof. Armitage. In the afternoon a service of son 5 entitled" Under the palms" will be given by the choir and Sunday school children. Primitive Methodist Syno d. The Primitive Methodists are holding their Synod at Warrington, commencing on Thursday next, and an interesting series of meetings has been arranged. The delegates will be received by the Mayor. and a welcome will also be extended td`them by a deputation from the Warrington Free Church Council on behalf of the Free Churches in the town.

Baptist Church, Colborne-street. Special Easter Services. Special services were held at the Baptist Church on Easter Sunday. In the morning the Rev. R. E. Letheren preached from John xx. 15-17, The promise of Easter" and his opening sentences gave the keynote to the services of the day." " Dawn! Spring ! Garden ! Angels !" That is the Easter environment! the fitting scenery and setting for Easter's supreme fact. The long night with its leaden footed hours, the long night through which the world waited for the light, has come to an end at last, and the new day has dawned that brings new hopes and possibilities. Life and immortality—life here with its mystery, life there with its boundless promise—have been 'brought to light with the dawning of Easter Day. Mr. Hughes was unfortun- ately prevented by influenza from fulfilling his promise to sing at the morning service. In the evening there was a capital congregation and the presence of Miss Bridge was greatly appreciated,and her fine rendering of "I know that my Redeemer liveth "was a contribution to the service that was greatly enjoyed. Mr. Letheren took for his text "If Christ be not risen " 1 Cor. 15-14. Is not this, be said, the biggest and the blackest " If" in the whole range of literature and life ? It seems almost incredible that in so little a word such large issues should be involved! A telling illustration then led to the statement of what must follow if Christ's resurrection is not a fact It is not one of the outworks of Christianity that is gone. The citadel is destroyed. It is not a solitary doctrine that is discredited. The very heart of it is gone. The problem of Easter was then stated; the fact of Christ's death emphasized ; the state of the disciples described. After a brief reference to the evidence for the resurrection of Christ, the preacher passed in rapid review various theories that have been proposed to account for the Christian facts, such as that Jesus did not really die, that the accounts were inspired only by visions, and showed how inadequate they were to satisfy the situation, that for his part he preferred rather to believe the supernatural than the ridiculous ! The sermon came to a close with a heart- felt assertion of the Resurrection as a fact for faith to 'fasten itself upon and find in it the explanation of the past, an experience for the present and an expectation for the future. The afternoon service was of a musical character the accompanist being Mr. Albert Trow. Solos were charmingly rendered by Misses Plinston and Woodland, and Mr. Wallington. The Chairman was Mr. Jones, Mr. Fernley offered prayer. The address was given by Mrs. Robert Letheren on "Music—a direct gift of God." She said we do not use the gift as we might in our homes or give it a sufficiently prominent place in our work; taking a circlet of verses, starting from I. Chron vi. 31., she took no the different ministries rendered by means of the gift of song. Poetry is the language of feeling and when poetry is wedded to music, it has wonderful power to stir the nobler impulses of our nature and to kindle a higher inspiration than that which comes to us from common things. The first illustrations of songs set to musical accompaniments were from the Book of Psalms and Song of Songs. The earliest example of song is found in Exodus xo. It follows the story of the wonderful deliverance of Israel from the land of Egypt, the power of Pharoah, when the children of Israel stand on the further shore of the Red Sea and look back upon the watery grave of their foes, then their thankfulness to God finds expression. Among the finest example of this service of song, we , may place the experience of Israel in exile in the land of Babylon and by its rivers, they sat down and wept as they remembered Zion; their conquerors taunted them and asked them to sing some of their songs of Zion, but their harps were hung upon the willows and their hearts too sad to sing ; but when the Lord turned their captivity their mouth was filled with laughter and their tongue with singing. Christian experience has its songs of liberty, &c. The gift of song has rendered noble service to the came of Patriotism, both to stir the heart to valiant deeds and to preserve noble memories. A great man once said he did not care who had the making of a nation's laws if he had the writing of its ballads. In former times the songs of minstrels served largely to preserve history. So in the Book of Deuteronomy Moses writes a song to he a witness of God's great deeds for His people. Ehenezer Elliott's Corn Law rhymes did as much on behalf of a cheap loaf as Cobden's speech. Since our citizenship is in heaven, and our real fatherland there too, let us make plentiful use of the songs of the Jerusalem above to nourish our patriotism for the heart's eternal home with God in the city which has foundations. Matthew Arnold sang Our lives are songs : God writes the words, And we set them to music at pleasure, And the song grows glad, or sweet, or sad, As we choose to fashion the measure. We must write the music whatever the song, Whatever its rhyme or metre, And if it is sad we can make it glad, Or if sweet, we can make it sweeter.

Bewsey-road Wesley Guild. Over 60 members of the Guild participated in an enjoyable ramble to Moore on Easter Monday after- noon. The party started from the church shortly after one o'clock. Tea was partaken of in the Wesleyan Schoolroom after which games were indulged in in a field kindly lent by Mr. John Rylands. Through the kindness of Miss Bessie Dutton the visitors were allowed to ramble through her grounds, and some • amusement was found by games of croquet on the: lawn. The Guild then sang several hymns in appre- ciation, and the homeward journey was commenced shortly after seven o'clock. Drunken Motor-car Driver. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, Thomas Broadbent Gregson, baker, of Lymm, was charged with being drunk in charge of a motor-car ' in Knutsford-road the previous night. Police-constable Lewis stated that he saw the prisoner driving the car in a zig-zag fashion. On stopping him he found prisoner under the influence of drink. When he got out of the car he fell to the ground. The car was travell- ing slowly at the time. The Chief Constable remarked that there were a number of convictions against the prisoner. The chairman (Mr. Henry Roberts) said the prisoner's record was as bad as it could be. A fine of 40s. and costa was imposed. Catholic Young Men's Society. A highly successful whist drive and dance promoted- by this society took place in the Co-operative Hall, I Sankey-street, on Monday evening, when about 140 ladies and gentlemen were present. The gentleman's prizelin the whist drive was won by Mr. George Dolan, after a draw with Mr. J. Blake. Messrs. Wilfred Rigby and E. Cross tied for the " booby " prize, but after " cutting " for it, it was awarded to Mr. E. Cross. The ladies' prize was won by Miss M. Riramer, and the " booby" prize by Mrs. Hardiman. . Hawing was indulged in until two o'clock on Tues- day morning, the music being supplied by Mr. Blake's band. The M.C.'s were Messrs. M. Cunningham, \V. Kilduff and G. Hearne. PUBLIC BENEFIT—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Warrington Male Voice Choir's Success. In the'chief male voice choir competition at Rhyl Eisteddfod on Monday, the Warrington Male Voice Choir, Connah's Quay, and Crewe Apollo entered for " The Martyrs of the Arena." All three gave brilliant renderings, and the prize was awarded to Warrington, conducted by Mr. Nesbit. The adjudicator (Dr. Rogers of Bangor) observed that while Welsh choirs usually gave more sympathetic renderings than English choirs, they were not always as accurate. -- On the return of the choir to Warrington a presentation of a large framed photo of the choir was made to Mr. J. ' H. Corrin, in recognition of the earnest and valuable work he has done during the years be has been a member.—Mr. Corrin, who is shortly leaving England, will do so with the best wishes of his comrades. Funeral of Mrs. Ernest Houghton. The funeral took place at Daresbury churchyard on Monday afternoon of Mrs. Ernest Houghton (wife or Mr. Ernest Houghton, of Moore), who died somewhat suddenly at 7.30 on Good Friday morning. The deceased lady was highly respected in the neighbour- hood, and there was a large gatheing of relatives and friends to witness the last rites, the service being ; conducted by the Rev. T. T. Lee-Jones, vicar, and the' Rev. J. 'S. Barnes, curate. The hymns "On the Resurrection morning" and "Jean, lover of my soul," were rendered by the Parish Church Choir, and as the body was-conveyed to the place of interment the organist (Mr. Wright) played the Dead March in " Saul. ' The deceased was 39 years of age. A large number of beautiful floral wreaths were sent as tributes of rear oct, including the following : "Husband, Noel and Raoul," members of Sankey Wire Mills Cricket Club, Miss B. Dutton, Mr. J. and R. Smith, Mr. and Mrs. W. Norbury. Mr. and Mrs. Sloane, Mr. and Mrs. W. Monks, "Edith and Box," Mr. and Mrs. S. Whitlow, " Edie and Alfred," Mr. and Mrs. Sherratt, Mr. and Mrs. Box, Mr. and Mrs. Herzog, Mrs. and Miss Smith (Penketh), " Nellie and Tom,' Mr. and Mrs. T.
